sections.title: A sequence is a function of its position & related topics

board_events.text: Think of the term as a function of its position: input $n$, output $a_n$.
A sequence is NOT a set: 1, 1, 2 keeps its order and its repeat.
Finite sequence ends; infinite sequence runs on forever.
A series is the running total of a sequence
Sequence 1, 2, 3, 4 becomes the series 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.
Sequences are about the terms; series are about the total.
Cricket: runs each over form a sequence; the score after $n$ overs is the series.
Finite series: finitely many terms. Infinite series: continued without end.
The index need not start at 1: a partial sum is $\sum_1^n - \sum_1^{m-1}$.
Golden habit: position → general term aₙ → then list or sum.
Sigma is shorthand for addition — with three algebra rules

board_events.text: Explicit rule gives $a_n$ directly; recursive rule needs seeds.
A rule must hold for ALL $n$ — three matching terms is only a conjecture.
To find aₙ from a pattern: constant differences → linear; constant ratios → GP.
Find the general term of 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, …
Check the differences first: 5, 7, 9, 11 — themselves an AP.
Constant SECOND differences ⇒ $a_n$ is quadratic in $n$.
Always verify a 4th term: a pattern is a conjecture until it holds.
Answer: aₙ = n(n + 2).
Write five terms: a₁ = 2, aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 1
Each term is built from the one before it — feed it forward.
Differences 5, 15, 45… and ratios both change — neither AP nor GP.
Recursion is Procedure 4: unfold terms one at a time.
Evaluate Σ (3k² − 2k + 1) from k = 1 to n
Split by linearity into three standard sums.
Split the sum, apply known sums — the engine of Unit 7.
Answer: n(2n² + n + 1) / 2.
Foundations — mistakes to hunt, habits to keep
Trap 1: confusing the nth term aₙ with the sum Sₙ.
Trap 2: declaring a general term from 3 terms without checking a 4th.
Trap 3: misreading the limits of $\sum$ (starting at 1 when it starts at 2).
Trap 4: treating a sequence as an unordered set, losing order/repetition.
Pro-tip: write $a_n$ FIRST, then decide — list, sum, or test for AP/GP.
To classify: differences constant → linear; ratios constant → GP.
Golden habit: position → general term aₙ → then list or sum.
Arithmetic progression: add the same step, over and over

Savings, stadium seating, auto-fare — all everyday APs.

Nearly every AP property is just a fact about straight lines.
Two board-derivable results you must reproduce

segments.text: Let's start at the very foundation. A sequence is just an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule, like the house numbers down one side of a street.
The order is everything here. The first term, the second, the third — each one sits in a fixed position that you cannot swap around.
Here is the picture to carry with you. A sequence behaves like a machine: you feed in a position, and it hands back the term that lives at that spot.
So install this habit right now — treat the term as a function of its position. Put in n, and out comes a sub n, the nth term.
<curious> There are two ways someone can hand you the rule. An explicit rule gives a sub n directly — like a sub n equals two n minus one, which prints one, three, five, seven.
A recursive rule instead builds each term from the earlier ones plus a seed value. Fibonacci is the classic: start with two ones, and every later term is the sum of the previous two.
<whisper> One quiet trap to remember. A sequence is not a set. One, one, two is a perfectly valid sequence, and both the order and the repeated one genuinely matter.
And finally, a finite sequence stops after finitely many terms, while an infinite sequence just keeps going without any end.
Now the second big idea. A series is what you get the moment you stop listing terms and start adding them up.
Take the simple sequence one, two, three, four. Turn the commas into plus signs and it becomes the series one plus two plus three plus four.
We write that compactly with the summation sign: a sub one plus a sub two, all the way to a sub n, equals the sum from k equals one to n of a sub k.
So keep the two ideas clean and separate. A sequence is about the individual terms; a series is about their total.
A cricket over makes this concrete. The runs scored in each over form a sequence, while the cumulative score after n overs is the series.
Just like sequences, series come in two flavours. A finite series adds finitely many terms; an infinite series continues its addition without end.
One notation point worth flagging. The index does not have to start at one. A partial sum from term m onward is just the whole sum up to n minus the whole sum up to m minus one.
And here is the golden habit for the entire chapter: go from position, to the general term a sub n, and only then decide whether to list the terms or sum them.
These are the tools that let you rearrange any sum, so let's meet them properly.
First, the sum of a sum splits apart. The sum of a sub k plus b sub k equals the sum of the a's plus the sum of the b's — you can separate the two families.
Second, a constant multiplier pulls straight out. The sum of c times a sub k is just c times the sum of a sub k.
Third, adding the same constant c a total of n times gives c times n — obvious, but it saves you every time a bare constant appears inside the sigma.
Reading a sigma is mechanical: read the index range, substitute each k, and add. The sum from k equals one to four of two k minus one is one plus three plus five plus seven, which is sixteen.
Two ways to define the underlying sequence carry over here. An explicit rule hands you a sub n directly; a recursive rule needs its seed values before it can generate anything.
<whisper> Now the trap that quietly ruins pattern problems. A general term must hold for every n. Fitting the first three terms is only a conjecture until the rule is stated and checked.
And a fast diagnostic for spotting the pattern: constant first differences mean a sub n is linear, and constant ratios mean it is geometric.
This one flips the direction — we are given the terms three, eight, fifteen, twenty-four, thirty-five, and asked to recover the rule.
The first move for any pattern is to look at the differences. Here they are five, seven, nine, eleven, and those differences themselves form an arithmetic progression.
That is the tell. When the second differences are constant, the general term must be quadratic in n — a formula built from n squared.
Working it out, the rule is a sub n equals n squared plus two n, which factors neatly as n times n plus two.
Let's confirm it. One times three is three, two times four is eight, three times five is fifteen — every term matches.
<whisper> And never skip this. A pattern is only a conjecture until you have verified it holds beyond the terms you used to guess it.
So the answer is clean: a sub n equals n times n plus two.
Here the rule is recursive, so we cannot jump straight to any term — we have to build them up in order. The seed is a sub one equals two.
The recipe is: each new term is three times the previous term, plus one. So we just feed the sequence forward, one step at a time.
From the seed of two, a sub two is three times two plus one, which is seven.
Continuing, a sub three is three times seven plus one, so twenty-two; then sixty-seven; then two hundred and two.
<curious> Now look carefully at what we built. The gaps are five, fifteen, forty-five — not constant — and the ratios shift too, so this is neither an arithmetic nor a geometric progression.
That is the real lesson of the example. Recursive sequences are their own thing; you unfold them term by term rather than reaching for a closed formula.
So the first five terms are two, seven, twenty-two, sixty-seven, and two hundred and two.
Now a preview of the summation engine we'll build in Unit seven. We want the sum from k equals one to n of three k squared minus two k plus one.
The key is linearity. A messy summand splits into three separate sums, each of which we can handle on its own.
So this becomes three times the sum of k squared, minus two times the sum of k, plus the sum of one.
Now plug in the standard results: the sum of k squared is n times n plus one times two n plus one over six, the sum of k is n times n plus one over two, and the sum of one is just n.
Doing the algebra, everything collapses to n cubed plus one half n squared plus one half n, which tidies up to n times two n squared plus n plus one, all over two.
<excited> That is the whole philosophy in one problem — split the sum, apply the sums you already know. This exact move powers the special-series unit later.
So the closed form is n times the quantity two n squared plus n plus one, divided by two.
Let's lock in the four traps that leak errors into everything downstream, then the one habit that prevents most of them.
The foundational trap, and the parent of countless later slips, is confusing the nth term a sub n with the running sum S sub n. Keep those two symbols crystal clear.
The second trap is over-fitting a pattern — declaring a general term from just three terms without ever checking a fourth. A pattern stays a guess until the rule is confirmed.
Third is a pure reading error: misjudging the limits of the sigma, for instance summing from one when the index actually starts at two.
Fourth is quietly treating a sequence as an unordered set, which throws away the order and any repeats that carry real information.
<curious> Now the pro-tip that dissolves most of these. Always write the general term a sub n first, and only then decide what to do with it — list it, sum it, or test it for AP or GP.
And to classify fast: constant differences tell you it is linear, while constant ratios tell you it is geometric.
Hold the golden habit above all: go from position, to the general term a sub n, and then choose to list or to sum. Get this reflex right and the whole chapter stops leaking.
Now the first real progression. An arithmetic progression is the mathematics of adding the same step, over and over again.
Picture a staircase where every step has exactly the same height. You start at floor level a, and each step lifts you by the same amount d.
That is the single defining property: the gap between consecutive terms never changes. That fixed gap has a name — the common difference d.
Written out, d equals a sub two minus a sub one, equals a sub three minus a sub two, and so on down the line — every consecutive pair differs by the same d.

<curious> And here is the beautiful part: after climbing n minus one steps from a, you are already standing at a plus n minus one times d. You have essentially derived the nth-term formula just by walking up the stairs.
These show up everywhere in daily life — fixed monthly savings, stadium seating that grows by a couple of seats per row, or an auto fare with a flat per-kilometre charge.
The deep idea to install early is that an AP is linear. Plot a sub n against n and the points land on a straight line whose slope is exactly d.
That one image explains almost every property we'll meet — because they are all just facts about straight lines wearing a disguise.
These two derivations are named, board-derivable results — examiners can ask for them line by line, so let's build them cleanly.
For the nth term, stack up the defining equations: each term equals the previous one plus d. Add all n minus one of them, and every interior term cancels telescopically.
What survives is beautifully simple: a sub n equals a plus n minus one times d. That is the workhorse formula of the whole unit.
The sum uses a different trick, the one the young Gauss reputedly used. Write the sum S sub n forwards, then write it again backwards underneath.
Now add the two lines column by column. Each of the n columns gives the same value, two a plus n minus one d, so twice S sub n equals n times that quantity.
Divide by two and you have it: S sub n equals n over two times two a plus n minus one d — and since the last term is l, that is also n over two times a plus l.
<excited> Feel the elegance here — pairing the first term with the last, the second with the second-last, every pair adds to the same total. That symmetry is the entire proof.
One quiet condition underlies both formulas: n must be a positive integer. If your algebra ever hands you a fraction or a negative n, that is a signal, not an answer.

sections.title: Arithmetic means and the Sₙ = An² + Bn test & related topics

board_events.text: Arithmetic mean, inserting means, and the sum test
Insert $m$ AMs between $a$ and $b$: the extended AP has $m + 2$ terms.

board_events.latex: S_n = An^2 + Bn \iff \text{AP, with } d = 2A,\; a_1 = A + B

board_events.text: The test needs ZERO constant term: $S_n = An^2 + Bn + c$ with $c \ne 0$ is NOT an AP.
Three-term test: $2a_2 = a_1 + a_3$ — needs no knowledge of $a$ or $d$.
When a sum is given, pick terms symmetrically

board_events.text: This turns a two-unknown system into one unknown instantly.
Even count uses common difference 2d, NOT d — a frequent slip.
AP 20, 19¼, 18½, 17¾, … — find a₂₈ and the first negative term
First negative term needs $a_n < 0$.
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ forces rounding UP: smallest integer is n = 28.
So the 28th term is itself the first negative term, equal to −¼.
Given a₁+a₅+a₁₀+a₁₅+a₂₀+a₂₄ = 225, find S₂₄
Equidistant property: $a_1 + a_{24} = a_5 + a_{20} = a_{10} + a_{15}$.
The six given terms pair into three EQUAL sums.
No need for $a$ or $d$ individually — linearity does the work.
Answer: S₂₄ = 900.
Two APs' sums are in ratio (7n+1):(4n+17). Find the ratio of 24th terms.
Standard device: ratio of $m$-th terms = ratio of $S_n$ at $n = 2m - 1$.
For the 24th terms, $m = 24 \Rightarrow n = 2(24) - 1 = 47$.
Why 2m−1? Because $S_{2m-1} = \tfrac{2m-1}{2}[2a + (2m-2)d]$ collapses to the mth term.
Answer: the 24th terms are in ratio 66 : 41.
Insert 11 AMs between 28 and 10; find the three middle means
The extended AP $28, A_1, \dots, A_{11}, 10$ has 12 gaps.
Eleven means is odd, so the three middle ones are $A_5, A_6, A_7$.
$A_6 = 19$ is the AM of 28 and 10 — the centre of a symmetric AP, as it must be.
Answer: the three middle means are 41⁄2, 19, and 35⁄2.
Saves ₹200/month for 3 months, then ₹40 more each month. When is total ₹11040?
Model the monthly savings as ₹200, 200, 200, 240, 280, … then sum.
Translating the word problem into $a$ and $d$ is the whole skill.
Summing all $n$ months gives a quadratic in $n$.
The ₹-savings archetype: reject the non-integer / negative root.
If log₂, log(2ˣ−1), log(2ˣ+3) are in AP, find x
Three terms in AP ⇒ middle is the AM of the outer two.
$2^x > 0$ rejects $u = -1$; never skip the domain check.
So $2^x = 5 \Rightarrow x = \log_2 5$.
S₇ : S₁₁ = 6 : 11, terms natural, 130 < a₇ < 140. Find d.
Terms are natural ⇒ d is an integer ⇒ $d = 9$ is forced.
Answer: d = 9 — the integer constraint does essential work.

segments.text: Now the means and one of JEE's favourite characterizations. If a, b, c are in AP, then b is the arithmetic mean of a and c — simply their average, a plus c over two.
That is the b equals a plus c over two condition, and it is the fastest three-term AP test there is.
To insert m arithmetic means between a and b, imagine an extended AP with those m means sitting between the endpoints — that is m plus two terms in total.
The common difference of that extended AP is b minus a over m plus one, and the k-th mean is a plus k times that step.
There is a lovely shortcut for their total: the sum of all m means equals m times the single AM of the endpoints, a plus b over two.

<curious> And here is the characterization examiners love. A sequence is an AP exactly when its sum has the form A n squared plus B n — and then the common difference is two A, with first term A plus B.

But watch the fine print carefully. The test demands a zero constant term. If the sum is A n squared plus B n plus c with c not zero, it is not an AP — only the terms from the second onward are. This is the single most punished trap on this formula.
Finally, the cleanest test of all: three numbers are in AP exactly when twice the middle equals the sum of the outer two — no need to know a or d at all.
Here is a technique that makes 'sum of terms' problems almost trivial. When a problem hands you the sum of some AP terms, choose them symmetrically about the middle.
The reason is visible on the board: if you place terms as a minus d, a, a plus d, the plus d and minus d cancel when you add, leaving a clean three a.
So for three terms, use a minus d, a, a plus d — their sum is simply three a, and one unknown vanishes on sight.
For five terms, extend the same idea outward: a minus two d, a minus d, a, a plus d, a plus two d, summing to five a.
<curious> The even case has a twist worth memorising. For four terms use a minus three d, a minus d, a plus d, a plus three d — and notice the common difference between them is two d, not d.
The payoff is huge: a system that looked like two unknowns collapses to one unknown the instant you switch to symmetric terms.
<whisper> But that four-term twist is exactly where students slip — the spacing there is two d, so never carry a bare d into the even case.
Let's start the AP examples with a board classic that hides a subtle integer step. The progression is twenty, nineteen and a quarter, eighteen and a half, and so on.
First read off the parameters. The first term a is twenty, and the common difference d is nineteen and a quarter minus twenty, which is minus three quarters — a decreasing AP.
For the twenty-eighth term, plug into the formula: twenty plus twenty-seven times minus three quarters. That is twenty minus eighty-one over four, which comes to minus one quarter.
Now the second question — the first negative term. We need a sub n to be strictly less than zero, so we solve the inequality.
Cleaning it up, the condition becomes eighty minus three times n minus one is less than zero, which gives n greater than twenty-seven and two thirds.
<whisper> Here is the careful part. Because n must be a natural number, we round up, not down — the smallest integer beyond twenty-seven and two thirds is twenty-eight.
So the two answers connect neatly: the twenty-eighth term is itself the very first negative term, and its value is minus one quarter.
This example rewards knowing one slick property instead of grinding algebra. We are told six scattered terms of an AP add to two hundred and twenty-five.

The key is the equidistant property. In any AP, terms equally spaced from the ends sum to the same total, so a sub one plus a sub twenty-four equals a sub five plus a sub twenty, equals a sub ten plus a sub fifteen.
Look at the six given indices: one and twenty-four, five and twenty, ten and fifteen. Each pair straddles the centre equally, so the six terms fall into three equal sums.
That means three times the quantity a sub one plus a sub twenty-four equals two hundred and twenty-five, so that pair-sum is seventy-five.
Now finish with the first-plus-last form of the sum. S sub twenty-four is twenty-four over two times a sub one plus a sub twenty-four, which is twelve times seventy-five, equal to nine hundred.

to first twenty-four terms ka sum nine hundred hai.
yah JEE Main ka favourite hai, aur poora khel ek substitution jaanne mein hai. humein do APs ke n terms ke sums ka ratio diya gaya hai, aur unke twenty-fourth terms ka ratio poocha gaya hai.
standard device yah hai: m-th terms ka ratio un sums ke ratio ke barabar hai jo n equals two m minus one par evaluate kiye gaye hon. yah term ratio ko sum ratio mein badal deta hai.
to hum bas a-m-one over a-m-two ke ratio ko un do sums ke ratio ke roop mein likhte hain, dono usi special index par liye gaye.
twenty-fourth terms ke liye, m hai twenty-four, to magic index hai two times twenty-four minus one, yaani forty-seven.

forty-seven ko diye gaye expression mein daalo: seven times forty-seven plus one over four times forty-seven plus seventeen, jo three hundred thirty over two hundred five hai, simplify hokar sixty-six over forty-one.

aur two m minus one kyon kaam karta hai? kyunki us index par sum factor two a plus two m minus two d rakhta hai — exactly m-th term ke core ka dugna — to ratio khud terms ke ratio mein simat jata hai.

extended progression socho: twenty-eight, fir eleven means, fir ten. yeh thirteen terms hain, aur crucially unke beech twelve equal gaps.

chunki eleven means ek odd count hai, ek genuine centre hai. beech ke teen means hain fifth, sixth, aur seventh.

board_events.text: The defining property: the RATIO between consecutive terms never changes.
Compound interest, depreciation, viral spread — all everyday GPs.
A GP is 'exponential': $\log a_n$ plots as a straight line.
$r > 1$: explosive growth. $0 < r < 1$: decay. $r < 0$: alternating signs.
An infinite AP always diverges; an infinite GP converges iff $|r| < 1$.
Two named results: the nth term and the sum of n terms
Each term is the previous times $r$, so telescoping the products gives:
For the sum, write $S_n$, then multiply the whole line by $r$.
If $r = 1$ every term is $a$, so $S_n = na$ — never divide by zero.
Interior terms cancel: only the first of one line and the last of the other survive.
The convergence condition, proved
When $|r| < 1$, each multiplication shrinks $r^{\,n}$ toward 0.
If $|r| \ge 1$, $r^{\,n}$ never vanishes — the sum diverges. This IS the proof.
A second pillar: for positive reals, $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$.
This chains further: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, with $AM \times HM = GM^2$.

segments.text: We finish the AP examples with a genuinely Advanced one, where an AP is reframed as a set of remainders. We intersect three infinite APs and are told the result is itself an AP.
The reframing is the key insight. Belonging to AP one with difference three means leaving remainder one on division by three, and similarly for the other two.
So a number lying in all three sets must satisfy three congruences at once: one mod three, two mod five, and three mod seven.
By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the numbers solving all three congruences themselves march along in a single arithmetic progression.
The common difference of that progression is the least common multiple of three, five, and seven, which is one hundred five.
Now we just need the first solution. Testing fifty-two: it is three times seventeen plus one, five times ten plus two, and seven times seven plus three — all three check out.

<excited> So the intersection is the AP with first term fifty-two and difference one hundred five, giving a plus d equal to one hundred fifty-seven. That is the AP-as-residue-class viewpoint the exam loves.
Let's close the unit by gathering the traps that quietly cost marks, then the shortcuts that win them back.
The number-one AP error is off-by-one: writing a plus n d instead of a plus n minus one d. Say 'n minus one' out loud every time.
The second big trap is the sum test. If the sum is A n squared plus B n plus a nonzero constant, the sequence is not a true AP — only the terms from the second onward behave.
Two more to watch: the even symmetric selection uses spacing two d, not d, and you must never assume the common difference is positive.
Also stay disciplined about roots. A non-integer n means there is no such term, and in log or quadratic problems, domain checks throw out extraneous roots.
<curious> Now the winning reflex. When a problem gives you a sum, switch to symmetric terms to halve the unknowns; when it gives you specific terms, stay with a plus n minus one d.
And keep the equidistant identity in your pocket — first plus last equals second plus second-last, and so on. It collapses scattered-term problems in a single line.
Finally, two lightning tests for whether something is an AP: check if the term is linear in n, or if the sum is quadratic with a zero constant. Master those and AP becomes almost mechanical.
Now the multiplicative twin of the AP. A geometric progression is the mathematics of repeated multiplication — of things that scale rather than step.

The classic Indian anchor is the chessboard: one grain on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, doubling all the way. That is a GP with first term one and ratio two, and the total exceeds all the wheat that ever existed.
That is the whole intuition — geometric growth feels tiny at the start and detonates at the end. The defining property is that the ratio between consecutive terms never changes.
Written out, r equals a-two over a-one, equals a-three over a-two, and so on. Every consecutive pair is scaled by the same factor r.
These are everywhere: compound interest growing your money, a bike depreciating in value, a rumour spreading through a class. All of them multiply by a fixed factor each period.
The deep idea, mirroring the AP's linearity, is that a GP is exponential. Plot the log of the terms and you get a perfectly straight line — which is exactly why logs turn a GP into an AP.

<curious> The sign of r changes the personality completely. r above one gives explosive growth, r between zero and one gives decay toward zero, and a negative r makes the terms flip sign, alternating up and down.
And here is the single most important structural contrast with the AP: an infinite AP always runs off to infinity, but an infinite GP settles to a finite sum exactly when the size of r is below one.
Let's build the two named GP results, both board-derivable. The nth term first, and it mirrors the AP derivation exactly, just with multiplication instead of addition.
Each term is the previous one times r: a-two is a r, a-three is a r squared, and so on. Telescoping those multiplications collapses everything to a single clean expression.
The result is a sub n equals a times r to the n minus one. That is the workhorse of the whole unit.
For the sum we use the signature trick. Write out S sub n as a plus a r plus a r squared, and so on, then multiply that entire line by r.

Now subtract the multiplied line from the original. Every interior term matches and cancels, leaving only a on one side and a times r to the n on the other, so S sub n minus r S sub n equals a minus a r to the n.
Factor and divide: S sub n equals a times one minus r to the n, over one minus r. Multiplying top and bottom by minus one gives the equivalent r-to-the-n minus one over r minus one form.
<whisper> But guard the denominator. If r equals one, that formula divides by zero, and the true answer is simply n times a, since every term is just a.
The elegance is the same as Gauss's reversal: shifting by one position makes the middle vanish, and only the endpoints of the two lines survive.
Now the result that separates a GP from an AP — the sum to infinity, and the proof of exactly when it exists.
Rewrite the finite sum by splitting the fraction: S sub n equals a over one minus r, minus a times r to the n over one minus r. The first piece is fixed; the second carries all the dependence on n.
Here is the whole argument. When the size of r is below one, every extra multiplication shrinks r to the n further, driving that second piece toward zero.
So in the limit, S sub n settles down to just a over one minus r. That is the celebrated sum-to-infinity formula, valid precisely when the size of r is under one.

<whisper> And this is not a side remark — it is the proof. If the size of r is one or more, r to the n never dies away, the limit fails, and the sum genuinely diverges. That is why the condition exists.
Let me also plant a second pillar we'll lean on constantly: the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality. It follows from one clean fact — the square of root a minus root b is never negative.
Expand that square and rearrange, and you get a plus b over two is at least root a b — the arithmetic mean is never below the geometric mean, with equality only when a equals b.
This chain extends all the way: arithmetic mean is at least geometric mean is at least harmonic mean, and beautifully, the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared.
Now the geometric mean and the inequalities that power every optimisation problem in the chapter.
If a, b, c are in GP, the middle term is the geometric mean of the outer two: b squared equals a c, so b is plus or minus the square root of a c.
For two positive numbers there is a single clean geometric mean, the square root of a b.
To insert n geometric means between a and b, the common ratio of the extended GP is b over a, raised to the power one over n plus one.
There is a lovely product rule for those means: the product of all n geometric means equals the single geometric mean raised to the n-th power — the multiplicative echo of the AP's sum-of-means rule.

<curious> And here is the workhorse inequality: for positive reals the arithmetic mean is always at least the geometric mean, with equality only when every number is equal. This one line settles a huge fraction of Advanced optimisation problems.

Handle the geometric-mean sign with care. It is plus or minus the root of a c, and you pick the sign that keeps the three terms a genuine GP — and for a real mean you also need a c positive, meaning same-sign endpoints.
Finally, the bridge you'll use again and again: taking logs turns a GP into an AP, because if a, b, c multiply geometrically, their logs step arithmetically.
This technique is the GP twin of the AP's symmetric selection, and it turns product problems into one-line algebra.
The picture on the board says it all: place terms as a over r, a, and a r, and when you multiply, the r in the denominator cancels the r on top, leaving a clean a cubed.
So for three terms in GP, always take a over r, a, a r. Their product is simply a cubed, and one unknown disappears immediately.
For five terms, extend outward with the same idea: a over r squared, a over r, a, a r, a r squared, multiplying to a to the fifth.

<curious> Now the even case, which hides a twist worth memorising. For four terms use a over r cubed, a over r, a r, a r cubed — and notice the ratio between these symmetric terms is r squared, not r.
The payoff mirrors the AP exactly: a two-unknown product problem collapses to a single unknown the moment you switch to symmetric terms.
<whisper> And that even-count ratio is precisely where students stumble — the spacing there is r squared, the perfect analogue of the AP's two-d trap. Never carry a bare r into the even case.

Let's open the GP examples with a board classic that rewards symmetric selection. The product of three GP terms is two hundred sixteen, and the sum of their pairwise products is one hundred fifty-six.
Immediately take the terms symmetrically as a over r, a, and a r — this is exactly what the technique is for.
The product is clean: a over r times a times a r is a cubed, and setting that to two hundred sixteen gives a equals six. One unknown gone.
For the pairwise products, factoring out a squared leaves a squared times one over r plus r plus one equals one hundred fifty-six, which reduces to one over r plus r equals ten thirds.
Multiply through and you get three r squared minus ten r plus three equals zero, which factors neatly as three r minus one times r minus three.
<curious> So r is either three or one third — but notice these give the very same set of numbers, just listed in reverse order.
Either way, the three numbers are two, six, and eighteen. Symmetric selection turned a two-unknown tangle into one clean quadratic.
This example reveals a hidden GP inside something totally familiar — a repeating decimal. We want to write nought point three recurring as an exact fraction.
The trick is to break the decimal into its place-value pieces, which turns out to be an infinite geometric series.
Written out, it is three tenths plus three hundredths plus three thousandths, and so on forever — each piece one tenth of the one before.
So the first term is three tenths and the ratio is one tenth. Crucially, the size of that ratio is well below one, so the infinite sum exists.
Apply the sum-to-infinity formula: three tenths over nine tenths, which simplifies to exactly one third.
<whisper> Notice what earned us the right to use the formula — the convergence check. The ratio is one tenth, comfortably under one, and only that check licenses the whole calculation.
The takeaway is worth carrying: every recurring decimal is secretly a convergent GP, so you can always convert one to a fraction this way.

<curious> And here is the workhorse inequality: for positive reals the arithmetic mean is always at least the geometric mean, with equality only when every number is equal. This one line settles a huge fraction of Advanced optimisation problems.

Handle the geometric-mean sign with care. It is plus or minus the root of a c, and you pick the sign that keeps the three terms a genuine GP — and for a real mean you also need a c positive, meaning same-sign endpoints.
Finally, the bridge you'll use again and again: taking logs turns a GP into an AP, because if a, b, c multiply geometrically, their logs step arithmetically.
This technique is the GP twin of the AP's symmetric selection, and it turns product problems into one-line algebra.
The picture on the board says it all: place terms as a over r, a, and a r, and when you multiply, the r in the denominator cancels the r on top, leaving a clean a cubed.
So for three terms in GP, always take a over r, a, a r. Their product is simply a cubed, and one unknown disappears immediately.
For five terms, extend outward with the same idea: a over r squared, a over r, a, a r, a r squared, multiplying to a to the fifth.

<curious> Now the even case, which hides a twist worth memorising. For four terms use a over r cubed, a over r, a r, a r cubed — and notice the ratio between these symmetric terms is r squared, not r.
The payoff mirrors the AP exactly: a two-unknown product problem collapses to a single unknown the moment you switch to symmetric terms.
<whisper> And that even-count ratio is precisely where students stumble — the spacing there is r squared, the perfect analogue of the AP's two-d trap. Never carry a bare r into the even case.

Let's open the GP examples with a board classic that rewards symmetric selection. The product of three GP terms is two hundred sixteen, and the sum of their pairwise products is one hundred fifty-six.
Immediately take the terms symmetrically as a over r, a, and a r — this is exactly what the technique is for.
The product is clean: a over r times a times a r is a cubed, and setting that to two hundred sixteen gives a equals six. One unknown gone.
For the pairwise products, factoring out a squared leaves a squared times one over r plus r plus one equals one hundred fifty-six, which reduces to one over r plus r equals ten thirds.
Multiply through and you get three r squared minus ten r plus three equals zero, which factors neatly as three r minus one times r minus three.
<curious> So r is either three or one third — but notice these give the very same set of numbers, just listed in reverse order.
Either way, the three numbers are two, six, and eighteen. Symmetric selection turned a two-unknown tangle into one clean quadratic.
This example reveals a hidden GP inside something totally familiar — a repeating decimal. We want to write nought point three recurring as an exact fraction.
The trick is to break the decimal into its place-value pieces, which turns out to be an infinite geometric series.
Written out, it is three tenths plus three hundredths plus three thousandths, and so on forever — each piece one tenth of the one before.
So the first term is three tenths and the ratio is one tenth. Crucially, the size of that ratio is well below one, so the infinite sum exists.
Apply the sum-to-infinity formula: three tenths over nine tenths, which simplifies to exactly one third.
<whisper> Notice what earned us the right to use the formula — the convergence check. The ratio is one tenth, comfortably under one, and only that check licenses the whole calculation.
The takeaway is worth carrying: every recurring decimal is secretly a convergent GP, so you can always convert one to a fraction this way.

sections.title: Infinite GP: sum 2, cubes sum 24 & related topics

board_events.text: Infinite GP has sum 2 and its cubes sum to 24. Find a and r.
The cubes form a GP with ratio $r^3$.
$(2r+1)(r+2)=0$: $|r|<1$ rejects $r = -2$, leaving $r = -\tfrac12$.
So $r = -\tfrac12$ and $a = 3$; check: $27 / (9/8) = 24\;\checkmark$.
First two GP terms sum to 12; third and fourth sum to 48; terms alternate in sign.

board_events.latex: a + a r = 12, \qquad a r^2 + a r^3 = 48

board_events.text: Divide the second equation by the first.
'Alternately positive and negative' forces $r < 0$, so $r = -2$.
Answer: first term $a = -4$.
Square of side 16 cm; join midpoints forever. Sum of all areas?

board_events.caption: Each inner square has half the area of the one outside it

segments.text: Here two infinite sums pin down a GP, and the convergence condition does the final selecting. The sum of the GP is two, and the sum of the cubes of its terms is twenty-four.
From the first fact, a over one minus r equals two, so a equals two times one minus r. That is our first relation.
Now the cubes. Cubing every term produces a new GP whose ratio is r cubed, so its sum is a cubed over one minus r cubed.
Setting that equal to twenty-four and substituting a cubed equals eight times one minus r cubed, the eights and a factor of one minus r cancel down nicely.

After simplifying with the difference-of-cubes factorisation, you land on one minus r squared over one plus r plus r squared equals three, which rearranges to two r squared plus five r plus two equals zero.
<whisper> That factors as two r plus one times r plus two, giving r equals minus one half or minus two. But the convergence condition rejects minus two outright, since its size exceeds one.
So the ratio is minus one half and the first term is three. A quick check confirms it: twenty-seven over nine eighths is indeed twenty-four.

This AIEEE problem shows how a single qualitative phrase can decide everything. The first two terms add to twelve, the third and fourth add to forty-eight, and we are told the terms alternate in sign.
Write both facts algebraically: a plus a r equals twelve, and a r squared plus a r cubed equals forty-eight.
The clean move is to divide the second equation by the first — the common factor of one plus r will cancel.
After cancelling, a r squared times one plus r over a times one plus r reduces to r squared, and the right side is forty-eight over twelve, so r squared equals four, meaning r is plus or minus two.
<whisper> Here the words do the work. Alternately positive and negative forces the ratio to be negative, so we discard plus two and keep minus two.
Now substitute back. With r equals minus two, a times one plus r is a times minus one, which equals twelve, so a is minus four.
So the first term is minus four. That one qualitative phrase — alternating signs — was the entire constraint that picked minus two over plus two.
Here is the geometry problem that makes convergence tangible. Start with a square of side sixteen centimetres, join the midpoints to make a second square inside, then repeat forever.
The board shows the nesting. The key geometric fact is that joining the midpoints of a square produces a new square with exactly half the area.
So the areas form a shrinking sequence, and we recognise it as a GP the moment we compute the first area.
The outer square has area sixteen squared, which is two hundred fifty-six square centimetres — that is our first term.
Each later area is half the one before, giving two hundred fifty-six, one hundred twenty-eight, sixty-four, and so on. So the ratio is one half, comfortably below one.
The total area is then two hundred fifty-six over one minus one half, which comes to five hundred twelve square centimetres.
<excited> Sit with how strange and beautiful that is — you nest squares infinitely many times, yet the areas add up to a perfectly finite number. That is the signature payoff of a convergent GP.
This is a signature Advanced technique — proving an inequality by multiplying two applications of AM ≥ GM. We must show the product of a-plus-b-plus-c and its reciprocal sum is at least nine.
The plan is to hit each factor with the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality on its own.
For the first factor, a plus b plus c is at least three times the cube root of the product a b c.
For the second factor, one over a plus one over b plus one over c is at least three times the cube root of one over a b c — the same inequality applied to the reciprocals.
<curious> Now multiply the two inequalities, both of whose sides are positive. The cube root of a b c and its reciprocal cancel completely, leaving nine on the right.
So the whole product is at least nine, exactly as required. This multiply-two-AM-GMs move appears again and again in Advanced problems.
And the equality tells you the extreme case: everything is tight precisely when a, b, and c are all equal.
This AIEEE problem has a wonderfully clean setup: in a GP of positive terms, each term equals the sum of the next two. We want the common ratio.
Because every term obeys the same rule, we can write the condition on just one representative term and its two successors.
That gives a equals a r plus a r squared. Dividing through by a, since a is nonzero, leaves one equals r plus r squared.
Rearranged, this is the quadratic r squared plus r minus one equals zero — short, but loaded.
The quadratic formula gives r equals minus one plus or minus root five, all over two.
<whisper> Now the positivity of the terms decides between the roots. The negative root would make terms negative, so we reject it and keep root five minus one over two.
And there is a lovely surprise in the answer: this value is exactly the reciprocal of the golden ratio, the number that shows up throughout nature and art.
We close the GP examples by returning to the chessboard legend and computing it exactly. One grain on the first square, doubling each square, all the way to the sixty-fourth.
The grain counts form a textbook GP — first term one, ratio two, and sixty-four terms in all.
Written out, the counts are one, two, four, and so on up to two to the sixty-third on the final square.
Apply the sum formula: a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one, which is one times two to the sixty-fourth minus one, all over two minus one.
Since the denominator is just one, the total is two to the sixty-fourth minus one — roughly one point eight times ten to the nineteenth grains.
<excited> That is a staggering number, and it makes the abstract point vivid: growth with a ratio above one truly detonates by the end, no matter how gently it starts.
To put it in perspective, that is more grains of wheat than have ever been grown in all of human history.
Let's gather the GP traps that quietly cost marks, and the shortcuts that win them back.
The number-one GP error, and the chapter's most punished slip, is writing the sum-to-infinity formula without first checking that the size of r is below one. Make that check a reflex.
Second, respect the sign of r. Dropping the negative-ratio, alternating-sign case loses whole problems, and picking the wrong sign when two roots survive is a classic slip.
Third, the geometric mean is plus or minus the root of a c — choose the sign that keeps a real GP. And never accept a solution that forces a term to zero, because a GP can never contain a zero.
Two more: the even symmetric selection uses ratio r squared, not r, and when r equals one the sum is simply n times a — do not blindly divide by r minus one.

<curious> Now the winning reflexes. Given a product, switch to a over r, a, a r to collapse the unknowns; and for any three-in-GP condition, reach straight for b squared equals a c rather than introducing a and r.
Keep the log bridge handy too — taking logs turns a GP problem into an AP problem, and the AP toolkit is often the easier one to swing.
And carry this recognition into the exam hall: every recurring decimal is a convergent GP in disguise, so you can always convert one to a fraction the instant you spot it.
Now the third classical progression, and it is really just the AP viewed upside-down. A sequence is in harmonic progression exactly when the reciprocals of its terms form an arithmetic progression.
The board shows the whole trick: flip every HP term over, and out comes a clean AP that you already know how to handle.
Written formally, a-one, a-two, a-three are in HP if and only if one over a-one, one over a-two, one over a-three are in AP.
Conceptually, the HP is the mathematics of rates over a fixed task — the place where the honest average stops being the arithmetic mean.

<curious> The classic anchor is a round trip. Drive out at forty and back at sixty over the same distance, and your average speed is not fifty but forty-eight — the harmonic mean, because equal distances make the rates combine harmonically.
Now a structural warning that surprises students. Unlike the AP and GP, the HP has no general formula for the sum of its terms. That is a genuine feature of the topic, not a hole in your memory.
One more fact to plant: the three means always line up in the same order — arithmetic at least geometric at least harmonic — coinciding only when all the numbers are equal.
Hold the master move above everything else: every HP question becomes an AP question the very instant you flip the terms over.
Let's start the HP examples with a clean computation that also verifies the key identity. We want the harmonic mean of four and twelve.
Apply the formula directly: two times four times twelve over four plus twelve, which is ninety-six over sixteen, giving six.
Now, to test the identity, let's also find the other two means of the same pair.
The arithmetic mean is four plus twelve over two, which is eight. The geometric mean is the square root of forty-eight, or four root three.
The identity claims the product of the arithmetic and harmonic means equals the geometric mean squared. So check the left side: eight times six is forty-eight.
And the right side: four root three, squared, is also forty-eight. The two match perfectly.
<curious> So the identity holds exactly, and that is worth keeping as a lightning self-check — any time you compute A, G, and H, confirm that A times H equals G squared.

board_events.text: 3rd term of an HP is ⅐, 7th term is 1⁄15. Find the 10th term.
Reciprocate: the reciprocals form an AP.
Flip back at the very end: the 10th HP term is $\tfrac{1}{21}$.
Answer: the 10th term is 1⁄21.
pth term of an HP is q, qth term is p. Find the (p+q)th and nth terms.
Reciprocate to an AP with first term $A_0$, common difference $d$.
A result worth memorising outright — it recurs across JEE Main.
Insert 4 harmonic means between 1 and 1⁄6
Insert 4 AMs between the reciprocals $\tfrac11 = 1$ and $\tfrac{1}{1/6} = 6$.
The HMs are the reciprocals of the interior AP terms.
Always work the means in the reciprocal AP, then flip back.
The AM of two numbers is 9 and their HM is 4. Find the numbers.
Use $AH = G^2$ to get the geometric mean first.
The means triad pins the numbers without ever solving the HM equation directly.
If a, b, c are in HP, prove a/(b+c), b/(c+a), c/(a+b) are in HP
Start from the definition: reciprocals are in AP.
Multiply through by the constant $(a+b+c)$ — still an AP.
Reciprocate that AP ⇒ $\tfrac{a}{b+c}, \tfrac{b}{c+a}, \tfrac{c}{a+b}$ are in HP. ∎
HP — the traps that cost marks, and the shortcuts that save them
Signature trap: attacking HP terms directly instead of reciprocating.
Missing '2': writing $\tfrac{ab}{a+b}$ instead of $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ for the HM.
Never invent a sum formula for an HP — there is none in general.
No zero terms allowed; reversing $A \ge G \ge H$ is a shared trap with Unit 5.
Pro-tip: reciprocate first, use the AP toolkit, flip back at the end.
For 'pth $=q$, qth $=p$', the answer is $a_n = \tfrac{pq}{n}$ — memorise it.
Remember HM ≤ GM ≤ AM: the HM is always the smallest, pulled toward the smaller number.
One number, three honest averages
AM = $\tfrac{a+b}{2}$ — the average when quantities ADD.
GM = $\sqrt{ab}$ — the average when quantities MULTIPLY (growth, CAGR).
HM = $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ — the average of RATES over a fixed task.

segments.text: This example is the reciprocate-first habit in pure form. We are given the third term of an HP as one seventh and the seventh term as one fifteenth.
The move is automatic: flip everything over, because the reciprocals of an HP form an arithmetic progression that we can attack directly.
So in the reciprocal AP, the third term is seven and the seventh term is fifteen.
The common difference is the change in value over the change in position: fifteen minus seven over seven minus three, which is eight over four, equal to two.
Now find the first reciprocal term: seven minus two times two is three. Then the tenth reciprocal is three plus nine times two, which is twenty-one.
<whisper> Here is the step students forget — flip back. We were working with reciprocals, so the tenth HP term is one over twenty-one, not twenty-one itself.
So the tenth term of the harmonic progression is one over twenty-one.
This is a JEE Main staple, and the reciprocate-first habit makes it almost trivial. The p-th term of an HP is q, and the q-th term is p.
As always, drop into the reciprocal AP. Call its first term A-nought and its common difference d.
The two facts become two clean AP equations: A-nought plus p minus one times d is one over q, and A-nought plus q minus one times d is one over p.
Subtract them and the d falls out beautifully — you find the common difference is one over p q, and the same value drops out for the first term A-nought.
So the n-th reciprocal is one over p q plus n minus one times one over p q, which collapses neatly to n over p q.
<curious> Flipping back, the n-th HP term is p q over n. And so the p-plus-q-th term is simply p q over p plus q — the whole messy problem in one line of AP algebra.
This answer is worth memorising outright. The p-th-equals-q, q-th-equals-p pattern recurs across JEE Main, and the clean formula a-n equals p q over n saves real time.
Inserting harmonic means is pure reciprocate-first. We must place four harmonic means between one and one sixth.
So we swing over to the reciprocal AP and instead insert four arithmetic means between the reciprocals — one over one, which is one, and one over one sixth, which is six.
The common difference of that reciprocal AP is six minus one over four plus one, which is exactly one — very clean.
So the reciprocal AP reads one, two, three, four, five, six, with the four inserted means sitting neatly in the middle.
Now flip back: the harmonic means we actually want are the reciprocals of those interior AP terms.
<curious> That gives one half, one third, one quarter, and one fifth — a satisfyingly tidy set of harmonic means.
The whole technique is the same every time: do all the mean-inserting in the reciprocal AP, then reciprocate the interior terms back at the end.
This example shows the three means working together as a team. We are told the arithmetic mean of two numbers is nine and their harmonic mean is four.
The clever first step is to route through the identity. The geometric mean squared equals the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean.
So G squared is nine times four, which is thirty-six, meaning the geometric mean is six. We now have all three means without touching the messy harmonic-mean equation.
The two means we care about give us a sum and a product: a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean, eighteen, and a times b is the geometric mean squared, thirty-six.
A sum and a product mean the numbers are roots of a quadratic: x squared minus eighteen x plus thirty-six equals zero.
Solving, x equals nine plus or minus the root of eighty-one minus thirty-six, which is nine plus or minus three root five.
<excited> Notice the elegance — the triad of means pinned the two numbers down without our ever having to solve the awkward harmonic-mean equation directly.

We finish the HP examples with a proof that showcases the signature reciprocate-and-manipulate chain. We must show that if a, b, c are in HP, then a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b are also in HP.
Begin from the definition. Because a, b, c are in HP, their reciprocals — one over a, one over b, one over c — are in AP.
Now the manipulation. Multiplying an AP by a nonzero constant keeps it an AP, so multiply through by a plus b plus c.
That gives a plus b plus c over a, over b, and over c — still an arithmetic progression.
Next, subtract one from each term. Subtracting the same constant from every term of an AP leaves an AP, and each term becomes b plus c over a, c plus a over b, a plus b over c.

<curious> Now reciprocate that AP one final time. The reciprocals of an AP form an HP, and those reciprocals are exactly a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b — which is what we wanted to prove.
That reciprocate-and-manipulate sequence is the signature HP proof technique: flip to an AP, scale and shift freely, then flip back.
Let's gather the HP traps that quietly cost marks, then the shortcuts that win them back.
The signature HP error is attacking the terms directly instead of reciprocating. If you find yourself grinding on the HP terms themselves, stop and flip.
The second trap is dropping the two: writing a b over a plus b for the harmonic mean instead of two a b over a plus b. That missing factor of two is a silent, plausible-looking mistake.
Third, never invent a closed-form sum for an HP. There genuinely isn't one, so if a question needs the sum, telescope it or sum termwise — we'll see that in Unit eight.
Two more: no term of an HP may be zero, and reversing the mean chain — writing H at least G at least A — is a trap shared with the next unit.
<curious> Now the winning reflex, and it is the whole subtopic: reciprocate first, run the full AP toolkit, and flip back only at the very end.
And memorise the p-q result outright — when the p-th term is q and the q-th is p, the n-th term is p q over n. It appears often enough to be worth instant recall.
Finally, keep the ordering in muscle memory: harmonic is at most geometric is at most arithmetic. The harmonic mean is always the smallest, pulled toward the smaller of the two numbers.
This unit ties the three classical means together. The key realisation is that there is more than one honest way to average two positive numbers, and each mean answers a different question.
The arithmetic mean, a plus b over two, is the right average when quantities add — marks, costs, distances.
The geometric mean, root a b, is the right average when quantities multiply. The average yearly return that turns one rupee into the same final corpus is the geometric mean, never the arithmetic one.
The harmonic mean, two a b over a plus b, is the right average of rates over a fixed task — the round-trip speed we met in the last unit.

The board shows the deep result: for two distinct positive numbers, these three always sit in the same order between a and b, with the harmonic nearest the smaller, the arithmetic nearest the larger, and the geometric in between.
<curious> So the ordering is fixed and strict: arithmetic above geometric above harmonic, collapsing to a single point only when the two numbers are equal.
And they are locked together by one identity: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared — which means the three means themselves form a geometric progression.
There is a lovely consequence hiding in that identity: the geometric mean is simultaneously the GM of the original pair and the GM of the arithmetic-and-harmonic pair.
Four short proofs hold this whole unit together, and none takes more than a line or two.

Start with the central identity. The arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean is a plus b over two, times two a b over a plus b — the a plus b factors cancel, leaving a b, which is the geometric mean squared.
Rearranged, that says A over G equals G over H, so the three means are in geometric progression with G as their middle term.

For the inequality, use the fact we planted earlier: the square of root a minus root b is never negative. Expand it and you immediately get a plus b over two is at least root a b — the arithmetic mean beats the geometric.

Now chain to the harmonic. Since H equals G squared over A, and A is at least G, dividing gives G squared over A at most G squared over G, which is G. So G is at least H, completing the chain A at least G at least H.
The fourth result recovers the original numbers from their means. We know a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean and a times b is the geometric mean squared.
By Vieta's formulas the numbers are roots of x squared minus two A x plus G squared, giving a and b equal to A plus or minus the root of A squared minus G squared.
<whisper> And here is the elegant twist. Those roots are real and positive exactly when A is at least G — so the discriminant condition is nothing other than the mean inequality itself.
Let's consolidate the compact formula set for two positive reals. Keep these together — they interlock.
The three means: arithmetic is a plus b over two, geometric is root a b, and harmonic is two a b over a plus b.
The core identity binds them: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, which is the same as saying the three means form a geometric progression.
The ordering is fixed: arithmetic is at least geometric is at least harmonic, with equality throughout only when the two numbers are equal.
To recover the numbers from their means, centre a quadratic on the arithmetic mean: x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero.
Its roots are a and b equal to the arithmetic mean plus or minus the root of the arithmetic mean squared minus the geometric mean squared.
<whisper> And carry the reality condition: real numbers exist exactly when the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean. If a problem hands you A below G, no such real pair exists.
Finally, everything generalises to n numbers: arithmetic mean is at least geometric mean is at least harmonic mean, with equality only when all the numbers are equal.

chunk_timeline.text: This example is the reciprocate-first habit in pure form. We are given the third term of an HP as one seventh and the seventh term as one fifteenth.
The move is automatic: flip everything over, because the reciprocals of an HP form an arithmetic progression that we can attack directly.
So in the reciprocal AP, the third term is seven and the seventh term is fifteen.
The common difference is the change in value over the change in position: fifteen minus seven over seven minus three, which is eight over four, equal to two.
Now find the first reciprocal term: seven minus two times two is three. Then the tenth reciprocal is three plus nine times two, which is twenty-one.
<whisper> Here is the step students forget — flip back. We were working with reciprocals, so the tenth HP term is one over twenty-one, not twenty-one itself.
So the tenth term of the harmonic progression is one over twenty-one.
This is a JEE Main staple, and the reciprocate-first habit makes it almost trivial. The p-th term of an HP is q, and the q-th term is p.
As always, drop into the reciprocal AP. Call its first term A-nought and its common difference d.
The two facts become two clean AP equations: A-nought plus p minus one times d is one over q, and A-nought plus q minus one times d is one over p.
Subtract them and the d falls out beautifully — you find the common difference is one over p q, and the same value drops out for the first term A-nought.
So the n-th reciprocal is one over p q plus n minus one times one over p q, which collapses neatly to n over p q.
<curious> Flipping back, the n-th HP term is p q over n. And so the p-plus-q-th term is simply p q over p plus q — the whole messy problem in one line of AP algebra.
This answer is worth memorising outright. The p-th-equals-q, q-th-equals-p pattern recurs across JEE Main, and the clean formula a-n equals p q over n saves real time.
Inserting harmonic means is pure reciprocate-first. We must place four harmonic means between one and one sixth.
So we swing over to the reciprocal AP and instead insert four arithmetic means between the reciprocals — one over one, which is one, and one over one sixth, which is six.
The common difference of that reciprocal AP is six minus one over four plus one, which is exactly one — very clean.
So the reciprocal AP reads one, two, three, four, five, six, with the four inserted means sitting neatly in the middle.
Now flip back: the harmonic means we actually want are the reciprocals of those interior AP terms.
<curious> That gives one half, one third, one quarter, and one fifth — a satisfyingly tidy set of harmonic means.
The whole technique is the same every time: do all the mean-inserting in the reciprocal AP, then reciprocate the interior terms back at the end.
This example shows the three means working together as a team. We are told the arithmetic mean of two numbers is nine and their harmonic mean is four.
The clever first step is to route through the identity. The geometric mean squared equals the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean.
So G squared is nine times four, which is thirty-six, meaning the geometric mean is six. We now have all three means without touching the messy harmonic-mean equation.
The two means we care about give us a sum and a product: a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean, eighteen, and a times b is the geometric mean squared, thirty-six.
A sum and a product mean the numbers are roots of a quadratic: x squared minus eighteen x plus thirty-six equals zero.
Solving, x equals nine plus or minus the root of eighty-one minus thirty-six, which is nine plus or minus three root five.
<excited> Notice the elegance — the triad of means pinned the two numbers down without our ever having to solve the awkward harmonic-mean equation directly.

We finish the HP examples with a proof that showcases the signature reciprocate-and-manipulate chain. We must show that if a, b, c are in HP, then a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b are also in HP.
Begin from the definition. Because a, b, c are in HP, their reciprocals — one over a, one over b, one over c — are in AP.
Now the manipulation. Multiplying an AP by a nonzero constant keeps it an AP, so multiply through by a plus b plus c.
That gives a plus b plus c over a, over b, and over c — still an arithmetic progression.
Next, subtract one from each term. Subtracting the same constant from every term of an AP leaves an AP, and each term becomes b plus c over a, c plus a over b, a plus b over c.

<curious> Now reciprocate that AP one final time. The reciprocals of an AP form an HP, and those reciprocals are exactly a over b plus c, b over c plus a, and c over a plus b — which is what we wanted to prove.
That reciprocate-and-manipulate sequence is the signature HP proof technique: flip to an AP, scale and shift freely, then flip back.
Let's gather the HP traps that quietly cost marks, then the shortcuts that win them back.
The signature HP error is attacking the terms directly instead of reciprocating. If you find yourself grinding on the HP terms themselves, stop and flip.
The second trap is dropping the two: writing a b over a plus b for the harmonic mean instead of two a b over a plus b. That missing factor of two is a silent, plausible-looking mistake.
Third, never invent a closed-form sum for an HP. There genuinely isn't one, so if a question needs the sum, telescope it or sum termwise — we'll see that in Unit eight.
Two more: no term of an HP may be zero, and reversing the mean chain — writing H at least G at least A — is a trap shared with the next unit.
<curious> Now the winning reflex, and it is the whole subtopic: reciprocate first, run the full AP toolkit, and flip back only at the very end.
And memorise the p-q result outright — when the p-th term is q and the q-th is p, the n-th term is p q over n. It appears often enough to be worth instant recall.
Finally, keep the ordering in muscle memory: harmonic is at most geometric is at most arithmetic. The harmonic mean is always the smallest, pulled toward the smaller of the two numbers.
This unit ties the three classical means together. The key realisation is that there is more than one honest way to average two positive numbers, and each mean answers a different question.
The arithmetic mean, a plus b over two, is the right average when quantities add — marks, costs, distances.
The geometric mean, root a b, is the right average when quantities multiply. The average yearly return that turns one rupee into the same final corpus is the geometric mean, never the arithmetic one.
The harmonic mean, two a b over a plus b, is the right average of rates over a fixed task — the round-trip speed we met in the last unit.

The board shows the deep result: for two distinct positive numbers, these three always sit in the same order between a and b, with the harmonic nearest the smaller, the arithmetic nearest the larger, and the geometric in between.
<curious> So the ordering is fixed and strict: arithmetic above geometric above harmonic, collapsing to a single point only when the two numbers are equal.
And they are locked together by one identity: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared — which means the three means themselves form a geometric progression.
There is a lovely consequence hiding in that identity: the geometric mean is simultaneously the GM of the original pair and the GM of the arithmetic-and-harmonic pair.
Four short proofs hold this whole unit together, and none takes more than a line or two.

Start with the central identity. The arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean is a plus b over two, times two a b over a plus b — the a plus b factors cancel, leaving a b, which is the geometric mean squared.
Rearranged, that says A over G equals G over H, so the three means are in geometric progression with G as their middle term.

For the inequality, use the fact we planted earlier: the square of root a minus root b is never negative. Expand it and you immediately get a plus b over two is at least root a b — the arithmetic mean beats the geometric.

Now chain to the harmonic. Since H equals G squared over A, and A is at least G, dividing gives G squared over A at most G squared over G, which is G. So G is at least H, completing the chain A at least G at least H.
The fourth result recovers the original numbers from their means. We know a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean and a times b is the geometric mean squared.
By Vieta's formulas the numbers are roots of x squared minus two A x plus G squared, giving a and b equal to A plus or minus the root of A squared minus G squared.
<whisper> And here is the elegant twist. Those roots are real and positive exactly when A is at least G — so the discriminant condition is nothing other than the mean inequality itself.
Let's consolidate the compact formula set for two positive reals. Keep these together — they interlock.
The three means: arithmetic is a plus b over two, geometric is root a b, and harmonic is two a b over a plus b.
The core identity binds them: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, which is the same as saying the three means form a geometric progression.
The ordering is fixed: arithmetic is at least geometric is at least harmonic, with equality throughout only when the two numbers are equal.
To recover the numbers from their means, centre a quadratic on the arithmetic mean: x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero.
Its roots are a and b equal to the arithmetic mean plus or minus the root of the arithmetic mean squared minus the geometric mean squared.
<whisper> And carry the reality condition: real numbers exist exactly when the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean. If a problem hands you A below G, no such real pair exists.
Finally, everything generalises to n numbers: arithmetic mean is at least geometric mean is at least harmonic mean, with equality only when all the numbers are equal.

inequality ke liye, wo fact use karo jo humne pehle boya tha: root a minus root b ka square kabhi negative nahi. ise expand karo aur tumhein turant milta hai a plus b over two kam se kam root a b — arithmetic mean geometric ko hara deta hai.

ab harmonic tak chain karo. chūnki H equals G squared over A, aur A kam se kam G hai, divide karne par G squared over A zyada se zyada G squared over G, yaani G. to G kam se kam H hai, chain A kam se kam G kam se kam H pūri.
chautha result original numbers ko unke means se recover karta hai. hum jaante hain a plus b twice the arithmetic mean hai aur a times b geometric mean squared.
Vieta ke formulas se numbers hain x squared minus two A x plus G squared ke roots, dete hain a aur b barabar A plus or minus root of A squared minus G squared.
aur yah raha elegant twist. vo roots real aur positive exactly tab hain jab A kam se kam G ho — to discriminant condition mean inequality ke alawa aur kuch nahi hai.
chalo do positive reals ke liye compact formula set consolidate karein. inhen saath rakho — ye aapas mein interlock karte hain.
tinoon means: arithmetic hai a plus b over two, geometric hai root a b, aur harmonic hai two a b over a plus b.
core identity inhen baandhti hai: arithmetic mean times harmonic mean equals geometric mean squared, jo yahi kehne jaisa hai ki teenon means ek geometric progression banate hain.
ordering fixed hai: arithmetic kam se kam geometric kam se kam harmonic, equality poori tarah sirf tab jab dono numbers barabar hon.
means se numbers recover karne ke liye, ek quadratic ko arithmetic mean par centre karo: x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero.
iske roots hain a aur b barabar arithmetic mean plus or minus root of arithmetic mean squared minus geometric mean squared.

aur reality condition le jao: real numbers exactly tab exist karte hain jab arithmetic mean kam se kam geometric mean ho. agar koi problem tumhein A, G se neeche de, to aisa koi real pair maujood nahi.
aakhir mein, sab kuch n numbers tak generalise hota hai: arithmetic mean kam se kam geometric mean kam se kam harmonic mean, equality sirf tab jab saare numbers barabar hon.

sections.title: Recovering the numbers from AM and GM & related topics

board_events.text: The AM of two positive numbers is 10 and their GM is 8. Find them.
Equivalently $a, b = 10 \pm \sqrt{100 - 64} = 10 \pm 6$.
$A = 10 > G = 8$, so real roots exist — the check is automatic.
Answer: the numbers are 4 and 16.

board_events.text: Apply AM ≥ GM to the two positive numbers $x$ and $\tfrac{9}{x}$.
Equality at $x = \tfrac{9}{x}$, i.e. $x = 3$ — the minimiser is the equality point.
Minimum value is 6.
For two distinct positive numbers, order A, G, H and name the GP
Distinct positives ⇒ the inequality is strict.
From $AH = G^2$, the triple $A, G, H$ is a GP.
So $A, G, H$ is a DECREASING GP whose middle term (GM) is $G$.
That $G$ is the very same GM of the original two numbers.
Two positives have AM = A and GM = G. Express them and find their ratio.
This comes straight from the recovery quadratic.
The ratio depends only on $A/G$, not on $A$ and $G$ separately.
The numbers are real iff $A \ge G$ — the same reality condition again.
A common Advanced form writes $A : G = (m+n) : 2\sqrt{mn}$.
Means relationship — the traps, and the fast moves
Direction trap: writing the chain backwards as $H \ge G \ge A$.
Reality: $A \ge G$ is exactly the real-roots condition for the board quadratic.
Centre the recovery quadratic on $A$, not on $G$.
Pro-tip: to find two numbers from means, jump to $x^2 - 2Ax + G^2 = 0$.
For min/max of $x + \tfrac{k}{x}$-type expressions, AM ≥ GM gives it in one line.
Equality $a = b$ always locates the optimiser.
Sanity check: $G$ is the middle term of the GP $A, G, H$ — a fast ordering test.
AGP: a GP whose terms carry a growing arithmetic label
