board_events.text: Present-value sums in finance are exactly AGP sums.
Neither the AP nor the GP sum formula works alone — but the GP trick does.
Multiply the whole sum by $r$, shift by one, subtract: the AP collapses to $d$.
When $|r| < 1$, the AGP converges: geometric decay beats linear growth.
Recognise an AGP by its shape: (linear in $n$) × ($r^{\,n-1}$).
The one technique that IS this subtopic
Subtract: every middle column leaves a clean $d\,r^k$.
Don't memorise the messy $S_n$ — re-derive with the subtraction every time.
Sum to n terms: 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + … (x ≠ 1)
Here $a = 1$, $d = 1$, $r = x$. Use multiply-by-$x$.
The interior GP $1 + x + \dots + x^{n-1}$ is what survives the subtraction.

segments.text: This is the signature board question for the unit — recovering two numbers from their arithmetic and geometric means. Here the arithmetic mean is ten and the geometric mean is eight.
Translate the means into a sum and a product. The sum a plus b is twice the arithmetic mean, so twenty; the product a b is the geometric mean squared, so sixty-four.
A sum and a product mean the two numbers are roots of a quadratic: x squared minus twenty x plus sixty-four equals zero.
This factors cleanly as x minus four times x minus sixteen, so the numbers are four and sixteen.
You can also read them straight off the recovery formula: ten plus or minus the root of one hundred minus sixty-four, which is ten plus or minus six.
<curious> And notice the reality check took care of itself — the arithmetic mean, ten, is comfortably larger than the geometric mean, eight, so real roots were guaranteed from the start.
So the two numbers are four and sixteen.
This shows why AM ≥ GM is the fastest optimisation tool in the chapter — no calculus required. We want the smallest value of x plus nine over x for positive x.
The curve on the board tells the story: it sweeps down to a single lowest point and back up, and we'll pin that point exactly with one inequality.
Apply the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality to the two positive quantities x and nine over x.
Their arithmetic mean is at least their geometric mean, and the geometric mean is the root of x times nine over x, where the x's cancel to leave just three.
Multiplying across by two, the expression x plus nine over x is at least six. We have the bound instantly.
<curious> And the equality condition hands us the minimiser for free. Equality in AM ≥ GM holds when the two quantities are equal, so x equals nine over x, giving x equals three.
So the minimum value is six, attained exactly at x equals three — no derivatives, just the mean inequality.
This example locks in both the ordering and the hidden progression among the means, for two distinct positive numbers.
Because the numbers are distinct, the mean inequality is strict — no ties are possible.
So the ordering is a clean, strict chain: the arithmetic mean is greater than the geometric, which is greater than the harmonic.
Now the structure. From the identity that A times H equals G squared, the three means themselves form a geometric progression.
Its common ratio is G over A, which also equals H over G, and since A is the largest, that ratio is below one.
<curious> So the means form a decreasing geometric progression, and its middle term — the geometric mean of A and H — is exactly G.
And here is the satisfying closure: that G in the middle is the very same geometric mean of the original two numbers we started with. The whole picture folds together neatly.
This Advanced example generalises the recovery, expressing the two numbers and their ratio purely in terms of their arithmetic and geometric means.
The numbers come straight from the recovery quadratic: a and b equal the arithmetic mean plus or minus the root of the arithmetic mean squared minus the geometric mean squared.
There is nothing new to derive here — it is exactly the roots of x squared minus two A x plus G squared, read off directly.
Their ratio is then the larger root over the smaller: A plus the root of A squared minus G squared, all over A minus that same root.

<curious> And here is the structural insight. If you divide top and bottom by A, the ratio depends only on the single quantity A over G — not on A and G separately. The shape of the pair is set entirely by how far apart the two means are.
Keep the reality condition in view: the numbers are real exactly when the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean — the same discriminant condition once more.
A common Advanced form writes the ratio of A to G as m plus n to two root m n, which is just this same relationship dressed in a substitution.
Let's close with the traps and the fast moves for the means relationship.
The single most common error is writing the chain backwards — harmonic at least geometric at least arithmetic. Fix the true direction in memory: arithmetic is the biggest.

Second, connect the reality condition to quadratics: A at least G is exactly the condition for the recovery quadratic to have real roots, because the discriminant is four times A squared minus G squared.
Third, centre that recovery quadratic on the arithmetic mean, not the geometric. The coefficient of x is minus two A, and the constant is G squared — mixing these up is a classic slip.
<curious> Now the pro-tips. To find two numbers from their means, jump straight to x squared minus two A x plus G squared equals zero — no need to reconstruct anything.
For minimum or maximum of x-plus-k-over-x type expressions, the arithmetic-mean geometric-mean inequality gives the answer in a single line, far faster than calculus.
And the equality case always locates the optimiser: the extreme is reached exactly when the two quantities are equal.
Finally, a fast sanity check on any ordering: the geometric mean must be the middle term of the geometric progression A, G, H. If it is not sitting in the middle, you have the order wrong.
Now a progression that fuses the two we already know. Think of an arithmetico-geometric progression as a GP whose terms are being steadily re-weighted by a growing counter.
The board makes it concrete. Take an AP on top, a GP below, and multiply them term by term — the geometric decay of r to the k multiplied by the linear march of the AP.
So the general term is a plus n minus one times d, all times r to the n minus one — the AP factor and the GP factor multiplied together.
This is not just an abstraction. Present-value and expected-value calculations in finance — steadily growing payments each discounted by a fixed factor — are exactly AGP sums.
Here is the defining challenge for summation: because each term carries both an additive and a multiplicative pattern, neither the AP sum formula nor the GP sum formula works on its own.

But the GP trick still works. Multiply the entire sum by r, line it up shifted by one position, and subtract. The arithmetic part collapses its differences into a single constant d, turning the leftover into an ordinary GP.

<curious> And convergence comes for free when the size of r is below one. Both r to the n and n times r to the n die away, because geometric decay eventually overwhelms the linear growth of the AP label, so the infinite sum is finite.
The recognition skill is everything: spot an AGP by its shape — something linear in n, multiplied by r to the n minus one.
This one derivation is the entire subtopic, so let's walk it carefully. It is the GP sum trick applied one level up.
Write out the sum S sub n: a, plus a plus d times r, plus a plus two d times r squared, and so on to the last term.
Now multiply the whole line by r, which shifts every term one position to the right — the same move we used for the plain GP.
Subtract the second line from the first. The first column gives a bare a, and every middle column leaves a clean d times r to the k, because the AP differences collapse to the constant d.
Collecting everything, one minus r times S sub n equals a, plus d times the geometric sum r plus r squared up to r to the n minus one, minus the final leftover term.

That inner bracket is just a GP sum, so dividing through gives the full closed form: a over one minus r, plus d r times one minus r to the n minus one, over one minus r squared, minus the last-term correction.

Letting n go to infinity with the size of r below one kills both the r-to-the-n-minus-one and r-to-the-n pieces, leaving the compact sum to infinity: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared.
<whisper> One piece of exam wisdom: don't memorise that messy finite formula. Re-derive it with the multiply-by-r subtraction every single time — it is faster and far more error-proof under pressure.
Let's open the AGP examples with the archetype — the sum of one plus two x plus three x squared, and so on to n terms.
Read off the parameters. The arithmetic labels are one, two, three, so a is one and d is one; the geometric factor is x, so r is x. Now apply multiply-by-x.
Write the sum S sub n as one plus two x plus three x squared, up to n times x to the n minus one.
Multiply the whole line by x, shifting each term right: x plus two x squared, and so on to n times x to the n.

Subtracting, the coefficients collapse. What remains is a clean geometric series — one plus x up to x to the n minus one — minus the single leftover n times x to the n. That geometric part sums to one minus x to the n over one minus x.
Dividing through by one minus x gives the closed form: one minus x to the n over one minus x squared, minus n x to the n over one minus x.
<curious> Notice what did all the work — the interior geometric progression is exactly what survives the subtraction, and summing it is the whole game.

Numerators 3, 5, 7, 9 form an AP ($a = 3$, $d = 2$).
Denominators 1, 2, 4, 8 form a GP with $r = \tfrac12$.
Separate numerator (AP) from denominator (GP) to read $a$, $d$, $r$.
Sum to n terms: 1 + 3x + 5x² + 7x³ + … (x ≠ 1)
Coefficients 1, 3, 5, 7 give $a = 1$, $d = 2$; $r = x$.
The last coefficient is $a + (n-1)d = 1 + 2(n-1) = 2n-1$.
Same method, just $d = 2$ instead of $d = 1$.
Evaluate Σ n²/2ⁿ from n = 1 to ∞
Split $n^2 = n(n-1) + n$ to reuse two standard sums.

AGP — the traps, and the fast moves

segments.text: This example rewards a clean first read — separating the arithmetic and geometric structure before touching the formula.
Look at the numerators three, five, seven, nine. They step up by two each time, so they are an AP with first term three and common difference two.
Now the denominators one, two, four, eight. They double each time, so they are a GP with ratio one half — and its size is safely below one.
So this is a genuine AGP with a equals three, d equals two, r equals one half. Apply the sum-to-infinity formula.
The first piece is three over one minus one half, which is six. The second is two times one half over one minus one half squared, which is one over one quarter, equal to four.
Adding, six plus four gives ten.
<curious> The key habit is that first split — read the numerator as the AP and the denominator as the GP, and the parameters a, d, and r fall out immediately, with no guesswork.
This Advanced example is the same machinery as before, but with a steeper arithmetic label to keep you honest about the constant d.
The coefficients are one, three, five, seven — odd numbers stepping by two — so a is one and d is two, while the geometric factor r is x.

Run the multiply-by-x subtraction. After lining up and subtracting, one minus x times S sub n equals one, plus two times the geometric block x plus x squared up to x to the n minus one, minus the last-term piece.
That geometric block sums to two x times one minus x to the n minus one, over one minus x, so we substitute it in.
Dividing by one minus x gives the closed form: one over one minus x, plus two x times one minus x to the n minus one over one minus x squared, minus two n minus one times x to the n over one minus x.

<whisper> Watch the last coefficient carefully. The final AP label is a plus n minus one times d, which is one plus two times n minus one, equal to two n minus one — not just n. Getting that wrong is the classic slip here.
So the method is identical to the archetype; the only change is carrying d equals two instead of d equals one throughout.
We close the AGP examples with a sum that looks harder than an AGP but yields to the same idea applied twice. We want the sum of n squared over two to the n, to infinity.
The trick is a clean split: write n squared as n times n minus one, plus n. This turns one awkward sum into two sums we already have formulas for.
The two standard results are: the sum of n times n minus one times r to the n is two r squared over one minus r cubed, and the sum of n times r to the n is r over one minus r squared.
For the first piece with r equal one half, two times one quarter over one eighth gives four.
For the second piece, one half over one quarter gives two.
Adding the two pieces, four plus two is six. So the sum of n squared over two to the n is exactly six.
<excited> That is the real power of the AGP machinery — iterated, it sums any polynomial-times-geometric series. Split the polynomial into building blocks and apply the standard sums one at a time.
Let's gather the AGP traps and the fast moves that beat them.
The dominant error is reaching for the wrong tool — trying the AP sum formula alone, or the GP formula alone, or the polynomial-sum method. Each handles only one half of an AGP.
Second, respect convergence: write the sum-to-infinity formula only after confirming the size of r is below one — the same discipline as the plain GP.
Third, mind the degenerate case. When r equals one, the AGP is really just an AP, so sum it with the AP formula and never divide by one minus r.
Fourth, don't swap the roles — be clear which factor is the arithmetic part and which is the geometric part, because mixing up d and r derails the whole calculation.
<curious> Now the pro-tips. Don't memorise the messy finite sum — re-derive it with the multiply-by-r subtraction every time. It is faster and far more reliable under exam pressure.
For the infinite sum, do memorise the compact form: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared. That one is short enough to trust.
And above all, train the recognition: an AGP is anything shaped like something linear in n, multiplied by r to the n minus one. Spot that shape and you know instantly which method to swing.
This unit is the computational engine of the chapter, and it rests on one move: break a complicated sum into simple sums you already know.

If you can write the general term as a combination of n cubed, n squared, n, and one, then by the linearity of the summation, the whole series is just the matching combination of the four standard sums.
The standard sums themselves come from a beautiful telescoping trick, shown on the board.

To find the sum of n squared, use the identity k cubed minus k minus one cubed equals three k squared minus three k plus one. Add it up for k from one to n and the left side collapses to just n cubed, leaving an equation you solve for the sum of squares.

<curious> And a point of real pride: the formulas for the sum of squares and the sum of cubes were first given by Aryabhata around four ninety-nine of the common era — over a thousand years before they appeared in European texts. When your students sum squares, they use an Indian result fifteen centuries old.
Here is a second intuition worth installing, also on the board: the sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n naturals.
So one plus eight plus twenty-seven is thirty-six, which is six squared, which is one plus two plus three, all squared. A startling, memorable coincidence.
The whole game is three steps: find the general term, express it in powers of n, and apply the standard sums.
Let's see exactly where the standard sums come from, and then a technique for recovering an unknown general term.
The engine is the identity k cubed minus k minus one cubed equals three k squared minus three k plus one — a simple algebraic expansion.
Now sum both sides for k from one to n. On the left, everything cancels telescopically except the very last k cubed, so the left side is simply n cubed.

That gives n cubed equals three times the sum of k squared, minus three times the sum of k, plus n. Substituting the known sum of k and solving hands you the sum of squares: n times n plus one times two n plus one, over six.
The very same machinery, using k plus one to the fourth minus k to the fourth, delivers the sum of cubes.
And that sum of cubes is the tidy square: n times n plus one over two, all squared — one identity generating the whole family.

<curious> The second tool is the method of differences, for when you are handed terms but not a formula. If the first differences of the terms form an AP, then the general term is one degree higher — a quadratic.

For example, three, seven, thirteen, twenty-one have first differences four, six, eight, ten, an AP, so the general term is quadratic — solving gives n squared plus n plus one, after which the standard sums apply.
Let's consolidate the four building-block sums and the master technique that ties them together.
The two simplest: the sum of r is n times n plus one over two, and the sum of one is just n.
The sum of squares is n times n plus one times two n plus one, over six — commit this to memory carefully.
The sum of cubes is n times n plus one over two, all squared — the same numerator as the sum of r, but squared.
The sum of fourth powers is rarely needed and only for Advanced: n times n plus one times two n plus one times three n squared plus three n minus one, over thirty.
Now the master technique. If the general term is a cubic polynomial in n — a n cubed plus b n squared plus c n plus d — then the sum is the matching combination of the standard sums, term by term.

<whisper> Here is the condition students forget: the technique only works when the general term is a polynomial. So a product like r times r plus one must be expanded into a polynomial first — never sum it as a product.
And for a sum that does not start at one, use the partial-range trick: the sum from m to n equals the sum up to n minus the sum up to m minus one.
Let's start the special-series examples with a product series. We want the sum to n terms of two times four, plus four times six, plus six times eight, and so on.
First find the general term. The r-th term is two r times two r plus two, which expands to four r squared plus four r — a clean polynomial.
Now apply linearity: the sum is four times the sum of r squared, plus four times the sum of r.
Substitute the standard sums: four times n times n plus one times two n plus one over six, plus four times n times n plus one over two.
Factor out the common two n times n plus one and combine what's left inside the bracket.
The whole thing tidies beautifully to four n times n plus one times n plus two, over three.

<curious> The one habit to internalise: expand the product into a polynomial first. Never try to sum a product like two r times two r plus two directly — the standard sums only apply once it is in powers of n.

So this is a genuine AGP with a equals three, d equals two, r equals one half. Apply the sum-to-infinity formula.
The first piece is three over one minus one half, which is six. The second is two times one half over one minus one half squared, which is one over one quarter, equal to four.
Adding, six plus four gives ten.
<curious> The key habit is that first split — read the numerator as the AP and the denominator as the GP, and the parameters a, d, and r fall out immediately, with no guesswork.
This Advanced example is the same machinery as before, but with a steeper arithmetic label to keep you honest about the constant d.
The coefficients are one, three, five, seven — odd numbers stepping by two — so a is one and d is two, while the geometric factor r is x.

Run the multiply-by-x subtraction. After lining up and subtracting, one minus x times S sub n equals one, plus two times the geometric block x plus x squared up to x to the n minus one, minus the last-term piece.
That geometric block sums to two x times one minus x to the n minus one, over one minus x, so we substitute it in.
Dividing by one minus x gives the closed form: one over one minus x, plus two x times one minus x to the n minus one over one minus x squared, minus two n minus one times x to the n over one minus x.

<whisper> Watch the last coefficient carefully. The final AP label is a plus n minus one times d, which is one plus two times n minus one, equal to two n minus one — not just n. Getting that wrong is the classic slip here.
So the method is identical to the archetype; the only change is carrying d equals two instead of d equals one throughout.
We close the AGP examples with a sum that looks harder than an AGP but yields to the same idea applied twice. We want the sum of n squared over two to the n, to infinity.
The trick is a clean split: write n squared as n times n minus one, plus n. This turns one awkward sum into two sums we already have formulas for.
The two standard results are: the sum of n times n minus one times r to the n is two r squared over one minus r cubed, and the sum of n times r to the n is r over one minus r squared.
For the first piece with r equal one half, two times one quarter over one eighth gives four.
For the second piece, one half over one quarter gives two.
Adding the two pieces, four plus two is six. So the sum of n squared over two to the n is exactly six.
<excited> That is the real power of the AGP machinery — iterated, it sums any polynomial-times-geometric series. Split the polynomial into building blocks and apply the standard sums one at a time.
Let's gather the AGP traps and the fast moves that beat them.
The dominant error is reaching for the wrong tool — trying the AP sum formula alone, or the GP formula alone, or the polynomial-sum method. Each handles only one half of an AGP.
Second, respect convergence: write the sum-to-infinity formula only after confirming the size of r is below one — the same discipline as the plain GP.
Third, mind the degenerate case. When r equals one, the AGP is really just an AP, so sum it with the AP formula and never divide by one minus r.
Fourth, don't swap the roles — be clear which factor is the arithmetic part and which is the geometric part, because mixing up d and r derails the whole calculation.
<curious> Now the pro-tips. Don't memorise the messy finite sum — re-derive it with the multiply-by-r subtraction every time. It is faster and far more reliable under exam pressure.
For the infinite sum, do memorise the compact form: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared. That one is short enough to trust.
And above all, train the recognition: an AGP is anything shaped like something linear in n, multiplied by r to the n minus one. Spot that shape and you know instantly which method to swing.
This unit is the computational engine of the chapter, and it rests on one move: break a complicated sum into simple sums you already know.

If you can write the general term as a combination of n cubed, n squared, n, and one, then by the linearity of the summation, the whole series is just the matching combination of the four standard sums.
The standard sums themselves come from a beautiful telescoping trick, shown on the board.

To find the sum of n squared, use the identity k cubed minus k minus one cubed equals three k squared minus three k plus one. Add it up for k from one to n and the left side collapses to just n cubed, leaving an equation you solve for the sum of squares.

<curious> And a point of real pride: the formulas for the sum of squares and the sum of cubes were first given by Aryabhata around four ninety-nine of the common era — over a thousand years before they appeared in European texts. When your students sum squares, they use an Indian result fifteen centuries old.
Here is a second intuition worth installing, also on the board: the sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n naturals.
So one plus eight plus twenty-seven is thirty-six, which is six squared, which is one plus two plus three, all squared. A startling, memorable coincidence.
The whole game is three steps: find the general term, express it in powers of n, and apply the standard sums.
Let's see exactly where the standard sums come from, and then a technique for recovering an unknown general term.
The engine is the identity k cubed minus k minus one cubed equals three k squared minus three k plus one — a simple algebraic expansion.
Now sum both sides for k from one to n. On the left, everything cancels telescopically except the very last k cubed, so the left side is simply n cubed.

That gives n cubed equals three times the sum of k squared, minus three times the sum of k, plus n. Substituting the known sum of k and solving hands you the sum of squares: n times n plus one times two n plus one, over six.
The very same machinery, using k plus one to the fourth minus k to the fourth, delivers the sum of cubes.
And that sum of cubes is the tidy square: n times n plus one over two, all squared — one identity generating the whole family.

<curious> The second tool is the method of differences, for when you are handed terms but not a formula. If the first differences of the terms form an AP, then the general term is one degree higher — a quadratic.

For example, three, seven, thirteen, twenty-one have first differences four, six, eight, ten, an AP, so the general term is quadratic — solving gives n squared plus n plus one, after which the standard sums apply.
Let's consolidate the four building-block sums and the master technique that ties them together.
The two simplest: the sum of r is n times n plus one over two, and the sum of one is just n.
The sum of squares is n times n plus one times two n plus one, over six — commit this to memory carefully.
The sum of cubes is n times n plus one over two, all squared — the same numerator as the sum of r, but squared.
The sum of fourth powers is rarely needed and only for Advanced: n times n plus one times two n plus one times three n squared plus three n minus one, over thirty.
Now the master technique. If the general term is a cubic polynomial in n — a n cubed plus b n squared plus c n plus d — then the sum is the matching combination of the standard sums, term by term.

<whisper> Here is the condition students forget: the technique only works when the general term is a polynomial. So a product like r times r plus one must be expanded into a polynomial first — never sum it as a product.
And for a sum that does not start at one, use the partial-range trick: the sum from m to n equals the sum up to n minus the sum up to m minus one.
Let's start the special-series examples with a product series. We want the sum to n terms of two times four, plus four times six, plus six times eight, and so on.
First find the general term. The r-th term is two r times two r plus two, which expands to four r squared plus four r — a clean polynomial.
Now apply linearity: the sum is four times the sum of r squared, plus four times the sum of r.
Substitute the standard sums: four times n times n plus one times two n plus one over six, plus four times n times n plus one over two.
Factor out the common two n times n plus one and combine what's left inside the bracket.
The whole thing tidies beautifully to four n times n plus one times n plus two, over three.

<curious> The one habit to internalise: expand the product into a polynomial first. Never try to sum a product like two r times two r plus two directly — the standard sums only apply once it is in powers of n.

board_events.text: First differences 4, 6, 8, 10 form an AP ⇒ $t_n$ is quadratic.
Evaluate Σ (1 + 2 + 3 + … + k) for k = 1 to 20
The inner sum is the triangular number $\tfrac{k(k+1)}{2}$.
JEE Main 2020: resolve the inner sum first, then apply standard sums.
Find $S_n$ for 5 + 55 + 555 + …
Each term is 5 times a repunit: $t_r = 5\cdot\frac{10^r - 1}{9}$.
Peel off the GP piece $10^r$ and the constant $-1$ separately.
A GP-based special series — geometric part summed, constant part is $-n$.
If $S_n = cn^2$ for an AP, find the sum of the squares of its terms
$S_n = cn^2$ is $An^2 + Bn$ with $B = 0$, so it's an AP.
Recover $a_n$ from $S_n$ via $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$, then square and sum.
Numerator is $\sum r^3 = \left[\tfrac{r(r+1)}{2}\right]^2$; denominator is $1+3+\cdots+(2r-1) = r^2$.
Both standard sums collapse the term to a clean quadratic before summing.
Special series — the traps, and the fast moves

segments.text: This example needs the method of differences, because we're given the terms with no formula in sight. The series is three, seven, thirteen, twenty-one, thirty-one.
Take the first differences: four, six, eight, ten. Those form an arithmetic progression, which is the signal that the general term is quadratic in n.
Fitting a quadratic to the first few terms gives the general term n squared plus n plus one. Check the fourth term: sixteen plus four plus one is twenty-one, which matches.
Now sum term by term using linearity: the sum of n squared, plus the sum of n, plus the sum of one.
Substitute the standard formulas: n times n plus one times two n plus one over six, plus n times n plus one over two, plus n.
Combining over a common factor, everything collapses to n times n squared plus three n plus five, over three.

<curious> And always verify with a small case. The sum of the first three terms should be three plus seven plus thirteen, which is twenty-three — and the formula gives three times nine plus nine plus five over three, also twenty-three. It checks.
This is a JEE Main problem that hides a sum inside a sum. We must evaluate the sum, for k from one to twenty, of the quantity one plus two plus three up to k.
The inner sum is a familiar object — the triangular number, k times k plus one over two. So substitute that in place of the inner expression.
The outer sum then becomes one half times the sum of k squared plus the sum of k, both taken from one to twenty.
Compute the sum of squares up to twenty: twenty times twenty-one times forty-one over six, which is two thousand eight hundred seventy.
Compute the sum of the naturals up to twenty: twenty times twenty-one over two, which is two hundred ten.
Adding those and halving: one half of two thousand eight hundred seventy plus two hundred ten is one thousand five hundred forty.

<curious> The lesson from this JEE Main favourite is to resolve the inner sum first — turn it into a clean polynomial in k — and only then bring in the standard sums. Nested sums are just two ordinary sums, one inside the other.
This example handles a series whose terms are made of repeated digits. We want the sum of five plus fifty-five plus five hundred fifty-five, and so on.
The key trick is rewriting each term. A repunit — a string of ones — equals ten to the r minus one, over nine. So the r-th term is five times ten to the r minus one, over nine.
Pull the constant five ninths outside, and the sum becomes five ninths times the sum of ten to the r minus one, for r from one to n.
Split that inside: the ten-to-the-r piece is a geometric progression summing to ten times ten to the n minus one over nine, and the minus one piece contributes a simple minus n.
Putting it together and simplifying, the sum is five over eighty-one times the quantity ten to the n plus one, minus nine n, minus ten.
<curious> The strategy generalises: when a series is built from repeated digits, peel off the geometric piece ten to the r and the constant separately, sum each on its own, and recombine.
So this is a geometric-based special series — the geometric part is summed with the GP formula, and the constant part simply contributes minus n.

This JEE Advanced problem links the sum-characterization back to special series. We're told the sum of the first n terms of an AP is c times n squared, and asked for the sum of the squares of those terms.
First, recognise the structure. c n squared is of the form A n squared plus B n with B zero, so this genuinely is an AP.
Recover the general term using the sum difference: a sub n equals S sub n minus S sub n minus one, which is c times n squared minus n minus one squared, giving c times two n minus one.
Now sum the squares: c squared times the sum of two n minus one squared, which expands to c squared times the sum of four n squared minus four n plus one.
Substitute the standard sums: four times the sum of squares, minus four times the sum of n, plus the sum of one, all scaled by c squared.
Simplifying the bracket, everything collapses to N times four N squared minus one, times c squared, over three.

<curious> The reusable move here is the recovery step — whenever you're given the sum but need the terms, take the difference of consecutive sums, and then the special-series machinery finishes the job.
We finish with an Advanced series where two standard sums appear inside a single term. The r-th term is the sum of cubes up to r, divided by the sum of odd numbers up to the r-th odd.
Simplify the two pieces. The numerator is the sum of cubes, which is r times r plus one over two, all squared. The denominator, one plus three up to two r minus one, is exactly r squared.
Dividing, the r squared cancels beautifully and the whole term collapses to r plus one, squared, over four — a clean quadratic.
So the sum is one quarter times the sum of r plus one squared, which we expand as one quarter times the sum of r squared plus two r plus one.
Substitute the standard sums: n times n plus one times two n plus one over six, plus n times n plus one, plus n, all scaled by one quarter.
Simplifying, the result is n times two n squared plus nine n plus thirteen, over twenty-four.

<excited> This is the signature special-series move — two known sums, one in the numerator and one in the denominator, collapse the ugly-looking term into a tidy quadratic, and from there the standard sums finish everything.
Let's gather the special-series traps and the moves that beat them.

The dominant error is formula confusion — swapping the sum of squares, with its over-six form, and the sum of cubes, which is a squared expression. Keep the three standard sums cleanly separated in memory.
Second is term recognition: you must find the general term as a polynomial before summing. A product like r times r plus one has to be expanded first — never summed as a product.
Third, watch the index range. When a sum doesn't start at one, use the partial-range correction: the sum up to n minus the sum up to m minus one.
Fourth, in the method of differences, don't mis-degree the term. Checking only the first differences when you should check the second is a common way to treat a quadratic as if it were linear.
<curious> The pro-tip is a single workflow that solves most problems: find the general term, expand it into powers of n, then apply the standard sums. Drill that sequence until it's automatic.
Keep the fastest shortcut ready: the sum of cubes equals the square of the sum. Recognise cubes on sight and you skip a whole computation.
And if you ever blank on the sum of squares, don't panic — re-derive it in four lines from the identity k cubed minus k minus one cubed. The telescoping origin is your safety net.
This final unit handles the sums that Unit seven cannot touch — where the general term is not a polynomial. The core idea is telescoping.
The picture says it all. A telescoping sum works like a collapsing telescope: each term cancels part of the next, so when you add everything, only the very first and very last pieces survive.
Formally, if you can write the r-th term as V-r minus V-r-plus-one, then the whole sum from one to n collapses to just V-one minus V-n-plus-one.
Think of a relay race where each runner hands off exactly what they received. Only the starting baton and the finish-line position matter; everything passed in between cancels in the bookkeeping.
The question is how to force a term into that difference-form. For a fraction, the tool is partial fractions.
For instance, one over r times r plus one splits cleanly into one over r minus one over r plus one — a perfect consecutive difference.
For products of consecutive integers, the tool is the V-n method — append a factor and divide. And for a surd in the denominator, you rationalise, which almost always produces a telescoper.
<curious> Keep the big picture: this unit is precisely the tool for non-polynomial general terms, exactly where Unit seven's standard-sum formulas break down.
Let's build the standard telescopers, and notice they all share one shape.
First, the workhorse. One over r times r plus one splits into one over r minus one over r plus one, and summing collapses to one minus one over n plus one, which is n over n plus one.

For the triple product, one over r times r plus one times r plus two, split it as one half times the difference of one over r times r plus one and one over r plus one times r plus two. The bracket telescopes.
Now the V-n method for a product. Take V-r as r times r plus one times r plus two. Then V-r minus V-r-minus-one works out to three times r times r plus one.
So r times r plus one is one third of that difference, and the sum telescopes to one third of n times n plus one times n plus two.
For factorials, notice r times r-factorial equals r-plus-one-factorial minus r-factorial. Summing that telescopes cleanly to n-plus-one-factorial minus one.
And for surds, rationalising one over root r plus root r plus one gives root r plus one minus root r — a difference ready to collapse to root n plus one minus one.
<curious> Feel the common thread: every single derivation is the same move — force the term into a difference of consecutive things, and then only the endpoints survive.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the telescoping toolkit — the principle first, then the standard results worth recognising on sight.
The principle is the whole unit in one line: if the r-th term is V-r minus V-r-plus-one, the sum is simply V-one minus V-n-plus-one.
The first standard result: the sum of one over r times r plus one is n over n plus one.
The triple-product sum is n times n plus three, over four times n plus one times n plus two.
For the odd-factor product, the sum of one over two r minus one times two r plus one is n over two n plus one.
The V-n method generalises the whole family: the sum of a product of k consecutive integers is the product of k plus one consecutive integers, divided by k plus one.
And two more to keep close: the sum of r times r-factorial is n-plus-one-factorial minus one, and the surd sum is root n plus one minus one.

<whisper> One warning that catches people out: track the constant multiplier. The triple product carries a one half, the odd-factor split carries a one half too — dropping that constant is a classic, silent slip.
Let's open the telescoping examples with the cleanest case — the sum of one over r times r plus one, and what it approaches as n grows.
The first move is partial fractions: one over r times r plus one splits into one over r minus one over r plus one.
Now write out the sum term by term: one minus one half, plus one half minus one third, and so on to one over n minus one over n plus one.
Look at what happens. Every interior fraction appears once with a plus and once with a minus, so they annihilate in pairs.
Only the outermost survivors remain: the leading one, and the trailing minus one over n plus one. So the sum is one minus one over n plus one, which is n over n plus one.
As n grows without bound, that trailing fraction vanishes and the sum approaches one.
<excited> So the infinite series one over one-times-two, plus one over two-times-three, and onward, equals exactly one — a beautifully clean result straight out of the collapse.
This example is the same idea with a twist — the denominators step by three instead of one, and a constant multiplier appears.
Read the pattern in the denominators: one and four, four and seven, seven and ten. So the r-th term is one over three r minus two, times three r plus one.
Partial fractions split this, but watch the constant: it becomes one third times the difference of one over three r minus two and one over three r plus one.
The bracket telescopes exactly as before, while the one third simply rides along on the outside of the whole sum.
After the interior terms cancel, we're left with one third times the quantity one minus one over three n plus one.
Simplifying, that is n over three n plus one.

<whisper> The one thing to guard here is that factor of one third from the split. Forgetting it gives a plausible-looking answer that's wrong by a factor of three — the telescope-lost-multiplier trap.
This example shows the V-n method at its cleanest, on a product of three consecutive integers.
Rather than expand into a cubic and sum term by term, we use the V-n shortcut, which mirrors how integration raises a power.
The general rule: the sum of a product of k consecutive integers equals the product of k plus one consecutive integers, divided by k plus one.
Here k is three. So we append one more factor — n plus three — and divide by k plus one, which is four.
That gives the sum directly as n times n plus one times n plus two times n plus three, over four.
Verify with n equals one: the sum should be one times two times three, which is six, and the formula gives one times two times three times four over four, also six. It checks.
<curious> The one rule to lock in is the divisor: you divide by the number of factors plus one. Using the wrong divisor is the classic V-n-method slip.
This example telescopes a factorial series with a small but clever rewrite of the numerator.
The trick is to split the numerator. Write r as r plus one, minus one — a harmless-looking move that unlocks everything.
Now r over r-plus-one-factorial becomes r plus one minus one, over r-plus-one-factorial, which separates into one over r-factorial minus one over r-plus-one-factorial.
And that is exactly a difference of consecutive reciprocal factorials — a telescoper in disguise.
Summing, all the interior terms cancel, leaving one over one-factorial minus one over n-plus-one-factorial, which is one minus one over n-plus-one-factorial.
As n grows, the trailing factorial term races to zero, so the infinite sum is exactly one.

<curious> The habit worth carrying: for factorial sums, look for a way to write the term as f of r minus f of r plus one, where f is some factorial expression. Once you spot it, the collapse is automatic.
This Advanced example telescopes a surd series, and the key move is rationalising the denominator.
Each term looks intimidating — one over root r plus root r plus one — but rationalising tames it completely.
Multiply top and bottom by root r plus one minus root r. The denominator becomes a difference of squares: root r plus one squared minus root r squared, which is just one.
So each term collapses to simply root r plus one minus root r — a clean consecutive difference.
Summing telescopes it: everything cancels except the endpoints, leaving root n plus one minus one.
Now evaluate at n equals ninety-nine: root of one hundred minus one, which is ten minus one, equal to nine.
<excited> That is the whole payoff — rationalising converted a sum of awkward-looking fractions into a clean telescoper, and a hundred-term sum came down to a single, tidy nine.
Let's close Unit eight with the telescoping traps and the fast moves that beat them.
The dominant error is failing to reach a difference-form at all — brute-forcing the sum, or trying to apply the polynomial standard-sum formulas to a fraction or a surd, where they simply don't fit.
Second is the endpoint sign. After collapse, the answer is V-one minus V-n-plus-one — not V-nought minus V-n. Off-by-one on the surviving endpoints is the main slip.
Third, don't lose the multiplier. When the split carries a one half or a one over k, that constant must ride all the way through to the final answer.
Fourth, in the V-n method, divide by the number of factors plus one — the wrong divisor quietly wrecks the result.

<curious> Now the decision tree. For a fraction, try partial fractions and look for a consecutive-shift difference. For a product of consecutive terms, use the V-n method. For a surd in the denominator, rationalise.
And for factorials, hunt for a way to write the term as f of r plus one minus f of r, with f a factorial expression.
Above all, remember the shape of every telescoping answer: it is always the first surviving term minus the last surviving term. If your answer isn't in that form, you haven't finished collapsing.
Here is your complete toolkit for the whole chapter, gathered on a single board. This is a recap — we're restating, not re-teaching, so let the formulas trigger the reasoning you already know.
Arithmetic progressions: the n-th term is a plus n minus one d, and the sum is n over two times two a plus n minus one d, or equivalently n over two times a plus last term.

Geometric progressions: the n-th term is a r to the n minus one, the finite sum is a times one minus r to the n over one minus r, and the sum to infinity is a over one minus r when the size of r is below one.
Harmonic progressions: reciprocate to an AP, the harmonic mean is two a b over a plus b, and remember the p-th-equals-q result, n-th term equals p q over n.
The means relationship: arithmetic at least geometric at least harmonic, the identity A H equals G squared, and recovery of the numbers as A plus or minus the root of A squared minus G squared.
Arithmetico-geometric progressions: the general term is a plus n minus one d, times r to the n minus one, with the compact sum to infinity a over one minus r plus d r over one minus r squared.
The special sums: the sum of r, the sum of r squared, and the memorable sum of cubes equals the square of the sum.
And telescoping: t-r equals V-r minus V-r-plus-one collapses to V-one minus V-n-plus-one, with the flagship sum of one over r times r plus one equal to n over n plus one.
<excited> That single board is everything the chapter rests on — carry it into the exam hall and every problem becomes a matter of choosing the right tool.

board_events.text: Write the first four terms of aₙ = (2n − 3)/4
Just substitute $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$ into the rule.
Terms −¼, ¼, ¾, 5⁄4 rise by ½ each — they form an AP!
Substitution is Procedure 1: from general term to terms.
Answer: the four terms are −¼, ¼, ¾, and 5⁄4.
Locked notation, and the four core formulas
$a$ = first term, $d$ = common difference, $l$ = last term, $S_n$ = sum.

board_events.latex: a'_n = l - (n-1)d \quad (\text{nth term from the end})

board_events.text: Off-by-one alert: it is (n − 1)d, never nd. Always say 'n minus one'.
d can be positive, zero, or negative — never assume $d > 0$.
First term $a \ne 0$, ratio $r \ne 0$: the core set
Never write $S_\infty = \tfrac{a}{1-r}$ without checking $|r| < 1$ first.
No term is ever zero, and $r \ne 0$: a GP cannot contain 0.
$r < 0$ ⇒ terms alternate in sign — neither increasing nor decreasing.
Two results that flow from reciprocating
If $a, H, b$ are in HP, then $\tfrac1a, \tfrac1H, \tfrac1b$ are in AP.
For 'pth term $=q$, qth term $=p$', work in the reciprocal AP.
The reciprocate-first habit turns messy HP algebra into one line of AP work.
Definition, nth term, means — all via the reciprocal AP

board_events.latex: a_n \text{ in HP} \iff \frac{1}{a_n} \text{ in AP} \;\;(\text{no zero terms})

board_events.text: HM uses $\tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ — the '2' is essential; and there is NO sum formula.
General term, both sums, and two must-know relatives
If $r = 1$ the AGP is just an AP — sum it with the AP formula, not this one.
These relatives also follow from differentiating the GP sum.
Sum to infinity: 1 + 2/3 + 3/3² + 4/3³ + …
Check $|r| < 1$ first, then plug into the two-term $S_\infty$.
Fast recall: one line per idea
AP: $a_n = a + (n-1)d$; test — $a_n$ linear, or $S_n$ quadratic with zero constant.
GP: $a_n = a r^{n-1}$; $S_\infty$ needs $|r| < 1$; for '$a,b,c$ in GP' use $b^2 = ac$.
HP: reciprocate → AP; $H = \tfrac{2ab}{a+b}$; no general sum formula.
Means: $A \ge G \ge H$; $AH = G^2$; recover via $x^2 - 2Ax + G^2 = 0$.
AGP: multiply by $r$, shift, subtract; $S_\infty = \tfrac{a}{1-r} + \tfrac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$.
Special sums: find $t_n$ → powers of $n$ → apply; shortcut $\sum n^3 = (\sum n)^2$.
Telescope: write $t_r$ as a difference; only $V_1 - V_{n+1}$ survives.
Golden habit throughout: position → general term $a_n$ → then list or sum.

segments.text: Let's put the machine to work on a clean board example. We are asked for the first four terms of a sub n equals two n minus three, all over four.
There is nothing subtle here — this is procedure one, from general term to terms. You simply substitute n equals one, two, three, and four into the rule.
Start with n equals one. Two times one is two, minus three is minus one, over four gives minus one quarter. That is our first term.
Carrying on the same way, n equals two gives one quarter, n equals three gives three quarters, and n equals four gives five over four.
<curious> Now notice something lovely. Those four terms climb by exactly one half each step, so they secretly form an arithmetic progression — a little preview of the next unit.
So the whole move was just substitution — the most basic habit in the chapter, and the one everything else is built on.
Our answer, cleanly stated: the first four terms are minus one quarter, one quarter, three quarters, and five over four.
Let's consolidate the notation and the formulas you will reach for constantly. This notation stays locked for the rest of the chapter.
The symbols are: a for the first term, d for the common difference, l for the last term, and S sub n for the sum of the first n terms.
The nth term from the beginning is a plus n minus one times d — the formula we just derived and the one you'll use most.
Sometimes it is cleaner to count from the end. The nth term from the end is l minus n minus one times d — the same structure, walking the other way.
The sum from first principles is n over two times two a plus n minus one d. Use this form whenever you know a and d.
When you happen to know the last term l instead, the sum simplifies to the lovely n over two times a plus l — first plus last, times how many pairs.
<whisper> Here is the single most common AP error to guard against. It is n minus one times d, never n times d. Whisper 'n minus one' to yourself every single time.
And one more caution: d can be positive, zero, or negative. Never quietly assume d is positive, or you will lose every decreasing-AP and first-negative-term problem.
Let's consolidate the GP formulas you'll reach for constantly. Two standing conditions frame them all: the first term is nonzero, and the ratio is nonzero.
The nth term is a times r to the n minus one — the exponential heartbeat of the whole unit.
Counting from the far end instead, the nth term from the end is the last term l divided by r to the n minus one — the same structure walked backwards.
The sum of n terms is a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one — or equivalently a times one minus r to the n, over one minus r. Pick whichever keeps your denominator positive.
And the crown jewel: the sum to infinity is a over one minus r, but only when the size of r is below one.
<whisper> Let me say the deadliest error out loud once. Never write the sum-to-infinity formula without first checking that the size of r is under one. It is the chapter's most punished slip.
Two structural facts to keep close. No term of a GP is ever zero, and the ratio is never zero — if your algebra forces a term to zero, an assumption was wrong.
And when the ratio is negative, the terms flip sign each step, so the sequence is neither increasing nor decreasing. Never silently assume the ratio is positive.
Let's derive the two HP results you'll lean on, and both fall straight out of reciprocating.
Take three numbers a, H, b in harmonic progression. By definition their reciprocals — one over a, one over H, one over b — are in arithmetic progression.
So one over H is just the arithmetic mean of one over a and one over b, which tidies to a plus b over two a b.
Flip that over and you have the harmonic mean of two numbers: H equals two a b over a plus b. Notice the two in the numerator — that is where students most often slip.
The second result is the famous set-up where the p-th term is q and the q-th term is p. The move is to work entirely in the reciprocal AP, never the HP itself.
Subtracting the two reciprocal-AP equations gives p minus q times d equals one over q minus one over p, which is p minus q over p q — so the common difference d is one over p q.
<curious> Back-substituting, the n-th reciprocal is n over p q, so the n-th HP term is p q over n. In particular, the p-plus-q-th term is p q over p plus q — a beautifully clean result.
The lesson beneath both derivations is one habit: reciprocate first. It turns messy HP algebra into a single line of routine AP work.
Let's consolidate the HP toolkit. Every formula here is really an AP formula seen through the reciprocal.
The definition anchors it all: a sequence is in HP exactly when the reciprocals of its terms are in AP — and, crucially, no term may be zero, since you cannot reciprocate zero.
The n-th term is one over the quantity one over a plus n minus one times d, where d is the common difference of that reciprocal AP.
For two numbers, the harmonic mean is two a b over a plus b — the single most-used HP formula.
For a whole list, the harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of the reciprocals — the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals.
To insert n harmonic means, insert n arithmetic means between the reciprocals of a and b, so one over H-k equals one over a plus k times D, with D the reciprocal-AP step.
And the bridge to the next unit: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, with the means ordered A at least G at least H.
<whisper> Two warnings to carry. The harmonic mean has a two on top — forget it and you get a wrong answer that looks plausible. And there is no sum formula for an HP; never invent one.
Let's consolidate the AGP formulas, plus two relatives that show up constantly in Advanced problems.
The general term is a plus n minus one d, all times r to the n minus one — the AP factor times the GP factor.
The sum of n terms is the three-piece expression we just derived: a fixed term, a geometric middle term, and a last-term correction. Use it, but be ready to re-derive it if memory wobbles.
The sum to infinity is the clean one worth memorising: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared, valid only when the size of r is below one.
Now the two relatives. The sum of n times r to the n is r over one minus r squared — the workhorse for polynomial-times-geometric sums.
And the sum of n squared times r to the n is r times one plus r, over one minus r cubed. Together these two handle a huge range of Advanced series.
<whisper> Guard the r-equals-one case. When r is one the AGP degenerates into an ordinary AP, so sum it with the AP formula — never plug r equals one into these expressions and divide by zero.
One elegant footnote: both relatives also fall out of differentiating the geometric-series sum, if you prefer the calculus route.
Now the compact infinite-sum formula in action. We want the total of one plus two thirds plus three over three squared plus four over three cubed, forever.

Read off the parameters: the numerators one, two, three, four give a equals one and d equals one, and the denominators are powers of three, so r is one third. Crucially, its size is below one, so the sum exists.
Apply the two-term sum-to-infinity formula: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared.
The first piece is one over one minus one third, which is three halves.
The second piece is one third over one minus one third, squared — that is one third over four ninths, which simplifies to three quarters.
Adding them, three halves plus three quarters is nine quarters.

<curious> And the discipline stays the same as with any infinite GP — check the size of r is below one first, then simply plug into the two clean terms. No multiply-by-r grind needed once you trust the formula.
Finally, the quick-recall cheat sheet — one line per idea, the kind of thing to skim minutes before an exam.
For arithmetic progressions: the n-th term is a plus n minus one d, and to test whether something is an AP, check that the term is linear in n, or that the sum is quadratic with a zero constant.
For geometric progressions: the n-th term is a r to the n minus one, the infinite sum needs the size of r below one, and for any three-in-GP condition reach straight for b squared equals a c.
For harmonic progressions: reciprocate to an AP, the harmonic mean is two a b over a plus b, and remember there is no general sum formula.
For the means: arithmetic at least geometric at least harmonic, the identity A H equals G squared, and recover two numbers from the quadratic x squared minus two A x plus G squared.
For arithmetico-geometric progressions: multiply the sum by r, shift, and subtract; and the compact infinite sum is a over one minus r plus d r over one minus r squared.
For special sums: find the general term, express it in powers of n, and apply the standard sums, with the shortcut that the sum of cubes is the square of the sum.
For telescoping: write the term as a difference of consecutive things, and only the first and last survivors remain.

<whisper> And carry the golden habit through everything: go from position, to the general term a sub n, and only then decide whether to list or to sum. Get that reflex right and the whole chapter is yours.

chunk_timeline.text: Let's put the machine to work on a clean board example. We are asked for the first four terms of a sub n equals two n minus three, all over four.
There is nothing subtle here — this is procedure one, from general term to terms. You simply substitute n equals one, two, three, and four into the rule.
Start with n equals one. Two times one is two, minus three is minus one, over four gives minus one quarter. That is our first term.
Carrying on the same way, n equals two gives one quarter, n equals three gives three quarters, and n equals four gives five over four.
<curious> Now notice something lovely. Those four terms climb by exactly one half each step, so they secretly form an arithmetic progression — a little preview of the next unit.
So the whole move was just substitution — the most basic habit in the chapter, and the one everything else is built on.
Our answer, cleanly stated: the first four terms are minus one quarter, one quarter, three quarters, and five over four.
Let's consolidate the notation and the formulas you will reach for constantly. This notation stays locked for the rest of the chapter.
The symbols are: a for the first term, d for the common difference, l for the last term, and S sub n for the sum of the first n terms.
The nth term from the beginning is a plus n minus one times d — the formula we just derived and the one you'll use most.
Sometimes it is cleaner to count from the end. The nth term from the end is l minus n minus one times d — the same structure, walking the other way.
The sum from first principles is n over two times two a plus n minus one d. Use this form whenever you know a and d.
When you happen to know the last term l instead, the sum simplifies to the lovely n over two times a plus l — first plus last, times how many pairs.
<whisper> Here is the single most common AP error to guard against. It is n minus one times d, never n times d. Whisper 'n minus one' to yourself every single time.
And one more caution: d can be positive, zero, or negative. Never quietly assume d is positive, or you will lose every decreasing-AP and first-negative-term problem.
Let's consolidate the GP formulas you'll reach for constantly. Two standing conditions frame them all: the first term is nonzero, and the ratio is nonzero.
The nth term is a times r to the n minus one — the exponential heartbeat of the whole unit.
Counting from the far end instead, the nth term from the end is the last term l divided by r to the n minus one — the same structure walked backwards.
The sum of n terms is a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one — or equivalently a times one minus r to the n, over one minus r. Pick whichever keeps your denominator positive.
And the crown jewel: the sum to infinity is a over one minus r, but only when the size of r is below one.
<whisper> Let me say the deadliest error out loud once. Never write the sum-to-infinity formula without first checking that the size of r is under one. It is the chapter's most punished slip.
Two structural facts to keep close. No term of a GP is ever zero, and the ratio is never zero — if your algebra forces a term to zero, an assumption was wrong.
And when the ratio is negative, the terms flip sign each step, so the sequence is neither increasing nor decreasing. Never silently assume the ratio is positive.
Let's derive the two HP results you'll lean on, and both fall straight out of reciprocating.
Take three numbers a, H, b in harmonic progression. By definition their reciprocals — one over a, one over H, one over b — are in arithmetic progression.
So one over H is just the arithmetic mean of one over a and one over b, which tidies to a plus b over two a b.
Flip that over and you have the harmonic mean of two numbers: H equals two a b over a plus b. Notice the two in the numerator — that is where students most often slip.
The second result is the famous set-up where the p-th term is q and the q-th term is p. The move is to work entirely in the reciprocal AP, never the HP itself.
Subtracting the two reciprocal-AP equations gives p minus q times d equals one over q minus one over p, which is p minus q over p q — so the common difference d is one over p q.
<curious> Back-substituting, the n-th reciprocal is n over p q, so the n-th HP term is p q over n. In particular, the p-plus-q-th term is p q over p plus q — a beautifully clean result.
The lesson beneath both derivations is one habit: reciprocate first. It turns messy HP algebra into a single line of routine AP work.
Let's consolidate the HP toolkit. Every formula here is really an AP formula seen through the reciprocal.
The definition anchors it all: a sequence is in HP exactly when the reciprocals of its terms are in AP — and, crucially, no term may be zero, since you cannot reciprocate zero.
The n-th term is one over the quantity one over a plus n minus one times d, where d is the common difference of that reciprocal AP.
For two numbers, the harmonic mean is two a b over a plus b — the single most-used HP formula.
For a whole list, the harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of the reciprocals — the reciprocal of the average of the reciprocals.
To insert n harmonic means, insert n arithmetic means between the reciprocals of a and b, so one over H-k equals one over a plus k times D, with D the reciprocal-AP step.
And the bridge to the next unit: the arithmetic mean times the harmonic mean equals the geometric mean squared, with the means ordered A at least G at least H.

Read off the parameters: the numerators one, two, three, four give a equals one and d equals one, and the denominators are powers of three, so r is one third. Crucially, its size is below one, so the sum exists.
Apply the two-term sum-to-infinity formula: a over one minus r, plus d r over one minus r squared.
The first piece is one over one minus one third, which is three halves.
The second piece is one third over one minus one third, squared — that is one third over four ninths, which simplifies to three quarters.
Adding them, three halves plus three quarters is nine quarters.

arithmetico-geometric progressions ke liye: sum ko r se multiply karo, shift karo, aur subtract karo; aur compact infinite sum hai a over one minus r plus d r over one minus r squared.
special sums ke liye: general term nikalo, ise n ki powers mein express karo, aur standard sums apply karo, is shortcut ke saath ki sum of cubes, sum ka square hai.
telescoping ke liye: term ko consecutive things ke difference ke roop mein likho, aur sirf pehla aur aakhri survivor bachte hain.
aur golden habit har cheez mein le jao: position se chalo, general term a sub n tak jao, aur tabhi decide karo ki list karna hai ya sum. wo reflex sahi kar lo aur poora chapter tumhara hai.
